danishChanges.before: 24. Og se nu på den anden side, på de sjældne tilfælde, jeg talte om, de mest fremragende idealister, der findes i dag blandt filosoffer og lærde. Har vi måske i dem fundet de eftersøgte modstandere af det asketiske ideal, dets anti-idealister? Faktisk tror de selv, at de er sådanne, disse »vantro« (for det er de allesammen): det synes, at denne idé er deres sidste rest af tro, idéen om at være modstandere af dette ideal, så alvorlige er de på dette emne, så lidenskabelige i ord og gestus; men følger det deraf, at det, de tror, nødvendigvis må være sandt? Vi »vidende« er gradvis blevet mistænksomme over for alle slags troende; vores mistanke har skridt for skridt vænnet os til at drage netop de modsatte konklusioner af, hvad folk har draget før; det vil sige, hvor end styrken af en tro er særligt fremtrædende, at drage konklusionen om vanskeligheden ved at bevise, hvad der tros, konklusionen om dens faktiske usandsynlighed. Vi benægter ikke igen, at »tro frembringer frelse«: af netop den grund benægter vi, at troen beviser noget — en stærk tro, der frembringer lykke, vækker mistanke om denne tros genstand, den fastlægger ikke dens »sandhed«, den fastlægger en vis sandsynlighed for — illusion. Hvad er nu stillingen i disse tilfælde? Disse i dag enspændte og fornægtere; disse fanatikere i én ting, i deres krav på intellektuel renhed; disse hårde, strenge, kontinente, heroiske ånder, der udgør vores tids ære; alle disse blege ateister, antikristne, immoralister, nihilister; disse skeptikere, »efektikere« og »hektikere« af intellektet (i en vis forstand er de de sidstnævnte, både kollektivt og individuelt); disse erkendelsens øverste idealister, hvori alene i dag den intellektuelle samvittighed bor og lever — de tror faktisk sig selv så langt væk som muligt fra det asketiske ideal, gør disse »frie, meget frie ånder«: og dog, hvis jeg må afsløre, hvad de selv ikke kan se — for de står for tæt på sig selv: dette ideal er simpelthen deres ideal, de repræsenterer det i dag, og måske ingen andre, de selv er dets mest spiritualiserede produkt, dets mest fremrykkede vagtpost af forposter og spejdere, dets mest insidious, delikate og elusiv form for forførelse. — Hvis jeg overhovedet er en gådelæser, så vil jeg være en med denne sætning: i nogen tid har der ikke været frie ånder; for de tror stadig på sandheden. Da de kristne korsfarere i Østen kom i sammenstød med denne uovervindelige assassinerorden, denne orden af frie ånder par excellence, hvis laveste grad lever i en disciplintilstand, som ingen munkeorden nogensinde har opnået, så på en eller anden måde fik de et nys om det symbol og kendetegn, der var forbeholdt den højeste grad alene som deres secretum, »Intet er sandt, alt er tilladt« — sandelig, det var tankefrihed, dermed blev der taget afsked fra selve troen på sandheden. Har sandelig nogen europæer, nogen kristen fritænker, nogensinde endnu vandret ind i denne sætning og dens labyrintiske konsekvenser? Kender han af erfaring Minotauros i denne hule? — Jeg tvivler på det — nej, jeg ved bedre. Intet er virkelig mere fremmed for disse »mono-fanatikere«, disse såkaldte »frie ånder«, end frihed og afsnører i den forstand; i intet henseende er de mere snært bundet, den absolutte fanatisme i deres tro på sandheden er uden sidestykke. Jeg kender måske alt dette for meget af erfaring på nært hold — denne værdige filosofiske afholdenhed, hvortil en sådan tro binder sine tilhængere, denne intellektets stoicisme, der til sidst nedlægger veto mod negation lige så stivnakket, som den gør mod bekræftelse, dette ønske om at stå stille foran det faktiske, factum brutum, denne fatalisme i »petits faits« (ce petit faitalism, som jeg kalder det), hvori fransk Videnskab nu forsøger en slags moralsk overlegenhed over tysk, denne afkald på fortolkning generelt (det vil sige, på at tvinge, lave om, forkorte, udelade, undertrykke, opfinde, forfalske og alle de andre væsentlige attributter ved fortolkning) — alt dette, bredt betragtet, udtrykker dydens askese, lige så effektivt som enhver afvisning af sanserne (det er i bunden kun en modus af denne afvisning). Men hvad der tvinger den ind i den ubetingede vilje til sandhed, er troen på selve det asketiske ideal, selv om den tager form af dets ubevidste imperativer — gør ingen fejl om det, det er troen, jeg gentager, på en metafysisk værdi, en iboende værdi af sandhed, af en karakter, som kun er garanteret og garanteret i dette ideal (den står og falder med dette ideal). Strengt bedømt eksisterer der ikke en videnskab uden sine »hypoteser«, tanken om en sådan videnskab er utænkelig, ulogisk: en filosofi, en tro, må altid eksistere først for at sætte videnskaben i stand til derved at vinde en retning, en mening, en grænse og metode, en ret til eksistens. (Den, der har en modsat opfattelse af emnet — han, for eksempel, der påtager sig at etablere filosofien »på et strengt videnskabeligt grundlag« — må først »vende på hovedet« ikke alene filosofien, men også selve sandheden — den groveste fornærmelse, der muligvis kunne tilbydes to så respektable damer!) Ja, der er ingen tvivl om det — og her citerer jeg min Den Glade Videnskab, jf. Bog V. aforisme 344: »Den mand, der er sandfærdig på den dristige og ekstreme måde, der er forudsætningen for troen på videnskab, hævder dermed en anden verden end den, der er livets, naturens og historiens; og for så vidt som han hævder eksistensen af den anden verden, kom, må han ikke ligeledes forkaste dens modstykke, denne verden, vores verden? Den tro, hvorpå vores tro på videnskaben er baseret, er forblevet til denne dag en metafysisk tro — selv vi vidende i dag, vi gudløse fjender af metafysik, også vi tager vores ild fra den brand, der blev tændt af en tusindårig tro, fra den kristne tro, som også var Platons tro, troen på, at Gud er sandhed, at sandhed er guddommelig... Men hvad nu, hvis denne tro bliver mere og mere utrolig, hvad nu, hvis intet beviser sig at være guddommeligt, medmindre det er fejl, blindhed, løgne — hvad nu, hvis Gud Selv beviser sig at være vores ældste løgn?« — Det er nødvendigt at standse på dette punkt og at overveje situationen omhyggeligt. Videnskab selv har nu brug for en retfærdiggørelse (hvilket ikke et minut er at sige, at der findes en sådan retfærdiggørelse). Vend dig i denne sammenhæng til de ældste og de mest moderne filosoffer: de undlader alle at indse omfanget af behovet for en retfærdiggørelse fra Sandhedsviljens side — her er et hul i hver filosofi — hvad er det forårsaget af? Fordi det asketiske ideal hidtil dominerede al filosofi, fordi Sandhed var fastlagt som Væren, som Gud, som den Højeste Appelret, fordi Sandheden ikke fik lov at være et problem. Forstår du dette »fik lov«? Fra det øjeblik troen på det asketiske ideals Gud forkastes, eksisterer der et nyt problem: problemet om sandhedens værdi. Sandhedsviljen havde brug for en kritik — lad os definere ved disse ord vores egen opgave — værdien af sandhed skal foreløbigt sættes i tvivl... (Hvis dette synes for lakonisk udtrykt, anbefaler jeg læseren atter at gennemlæse den passage fra Den Glade Videnskab, der bærer titlen, »Hvor langt vi også stadig er fromme«, aforisme 344, og bedst af alt hele den femte bog af det værk, samt forordet til Morgenrødens Daggry.)

Bog V. aforisme 344: »Den mand, der er sandfærdig på den dristige og ekstreme måde, der er forudsætningen for troen på videnskab, hævder dermed en anden verden end den, der er livets, naturens og historiens; og for så vidt som han hævder eksistensen af den anden verden, må han så ikke ligeledes forkaste dens modstykke, denne verden, vores verden? Den tro, hvorpå vores tro på videnskaben er baseret, er forblevet til denne dag en metafysisk tro — selv vi erkendende i dag, vi gudløse fjender af metafysik, også vi tager vores ild fra den brand, der blev tændt af en tusindårig tro, fra den kristne tro, som også var Platons tro, troen på, at Gud er sandhed, at sandhed er guddommelig... Men hvad nu, hvis denne tro bliver mere og mere utrolig, hvad nu, hvis intet beviser sig at være guddommeligt, medmindre det er fejl, blindhed, løgne — hvad nu, hvis Gud Selv beviser sig at være vores ældste løgn?« — Det er nødvendigt at standse på dette punkt og at overveje situationen omhyggeligt. Videnskab selv har nu brug for en retfærdiggørelse (hvilket bestemt ikke betyder, at der findes en sådan retfærdiggørelse). Vend dig i denne sammenhæng til de ældste og de mest moderne filosoffer: de undlader alle at indse omfanget af behovet for en retfærdiggørelse fra Sandhedsviljens side — her er et hul i hver filosofi — hvad er det forårsaget af? Fordi det asketiske ideal hidtil dominerede al filosofi, fordi Sandhed var fastlagt som Væren, som Gud, som den højeste instans, fordi Sandheden ikke fik lov at være et problem. Forstår du dette »fik lov«? Fra det øjeblik troen på det asketiske ideals Gud forkastes, eksisterer der et nyt problem: problemet om sandhedens værdi. Sandhedsviljen havde brug for en kritik — lad os definere ved disse ord vores egen opgave — værdien af sandhed skal foreløbigt sættes i tvivl... (Hvis dette synes for lakonisk udtrykt, anbefaler jeg læseren atter at gennemlæse den passage fra Den Glade Videnskab, der bærer titlen, »Hvor langt vi også stadig er fromme«, aforisme 344, og bedst af alt hele den femte bog af det værk, samt forordet til Morgenrøde.)

danishChanges.before: 25. Nej! Du kan ikke komme uden om mig med videnskab, når jeg søger de naturlige modstandere af det asketiske ideal, når jeg stiller spørgsmålet: »Hvor er den modsatte vilje, hvori modstanderidealet udtrykker sig?« Videnskab er ikke, langtfra, uafhængig nok til at opfylde denne funktion; i hver afdeling har videnskaben brug for en idealværdi, en magt der skaber værdier, og i hvis tjeneste den kan tro på sig selv — videnskaben selv skaber aldrig værdier. Dens forhold til det asketiske ideal er ikke i sig selv antagonistisk; groft sagt repræsenterer den snarere den progressive kraft i den indre udvikling af dette ideal. Mere nøje undersøgt, dens modstand og antagonisme drejer sig ikke om selve idealet, men kun om dette ideals udposter, dets ydre dragt, dets maskerade, med dets midlertidige hærdning, stivning og dogmatisering — den frigør livet i idealet endnu engang, mens den forkaster dets overfladiske elementer. Disse to fænomener, videnskaben og det asketiske ideal, hviler begge på samme grundlag — jeg har allerede gjort dette klart — grundlaget, siger jeg, af den samme overvurdering af sandhed (mere præcist samme tro på umuligheden af at vurdere og kritisere sandheden), og følgelig er de nødvendigvis allierede, så hvis de bliver angrebet, må de altid angribes og kaldes i tvivl sammen. En vurdering af det asketiske ideal medfører uundgåeligt også en vurdering af videnskaben; spild ingen tid på at se dette klart, og vær skarp til at fange det! (Kunst, jeg taler foreløbigt, for jeg vil behandle den ved en anden lejlighed mere detaljeret — kunst, gentager jeg, hvori løgn helliges, og viljen til bedrag har god samvittighed på sin side, er meget mere fundamentalt modsat det asketiske ideal end videnskab er: Platons instinkt fornemmede dette — Platon, den største kunstfjende, Europa har frembragt indtil nu. Platon contra Homer, det er den fuldstændige, den sande antagonisme — på den ene side den helhjertede »transcendentale«, den store bagvasker af livet; på den anden side dets ufrivillige lovpriser, den gyldne natur. En kunstnerisk tjenstvillighed til det asketiske ideals tjeneste er følgelig den mest absolutte kunstneriske korruption, der findes, skønt det desværre er en af de hyppigste faser, for intet er mere korrumperbart end en kunstner.) Fysiologisk betragtet hviler videnskaben endvidere på samme grundlag som det asketiske ideal: en vis livets forarmelse er forudsætningen for sidstnævnte som for førstnævnte — tilføj følelsernes frigiditet, tempoets nedslapning, dialektikkens substitution for instinkt, alvor præget på mine og gestus (alvor, det mest umiskendelige tegn på anstrengt stofskifte, på kæmpende, stridende liv). Betragt perioderne i en nation, hvori den lærde mand træder i forgrunden; det er udmattelsens, ofte solnedgangens, forfaldets perioder — den boblende styrke, tilliden til livet, tilliden til fremtiden er ikke længere. De mandariners overvægt betyder aldrig noget godt, lige så lidt som demokratiets fremkomst eller voldgift i stedet for krig, lige rettigheder for kvinder, medlidenhedens religion og alle de andre symptomer på dalende liv. (Videnskab håndteret som problem! hvad betyder videnskab? — på dette punkt forordet til Tragediens Fødsel.) Nej! denne »moderne videnskab« — mærk dig dette godt — er til tider den bedste allierede for det asketiske ideal, og af netop den grund, at den er den allierede, der er mest ubevidst, mest automatisk, mest hemmelig og mest underjordisk! De har spillet hinanden i hænde indtil nu, har disse »fattige i ånden« og det ideals videnskabelige modstandere (pas på, for øvrigt, ikke at tro, at disse modstandere er antitesen til dette ideal, at de er de rige i ånden — det er de ikke; jeg har kaldt dem de hektiske i ånden). Hvad angår disse berømte sejre for videnskaben: der er ingen tvivl om, at de er sejre — men sejre over hvad? Der var ikke et eneste minut nogen sejr i deres liste over det asketiske ideal, snarere blev det stærkere, det vil sige, mere elusiv, mere abstrakt, mere insidious, ud fra det faktum, at en mur, en udpost, der var blevet bygget på til hovedfæstningen og forvansket dens udseende, fra tid til anden skulle hensynsløst ødelægges og brydes ned af videnskaben. Foreslår nogen seriøst, at den teologiske astronomis fald betød faldet af det ideal? — Er måske mennesket blevet mindre i behov af en transcendental løsning på sin tilværelses gåde, fordi denne tilværelse siden den tid er blevet mere tilfældig, lejlighedsvis og overflødig i universets synlige orden? Har der ikke siden Kopernikus' tid været en uafbrudt fremgang i menneskets selvforringelse og hans vilje til at forringe sig selv? Ak, hans tro på sin værdighed, sin enestående, uerstattelighed i tilværelsens skema, er væk — han er blevet dyr, bogstaveligt, ubetinget og ufordømmeligt dyr, han, der i sin tidligere tro var næsten Gud (»Guds barn«, »halvgud«). Siden Kopernikus synes mennesket at være faldet på et stejlt plan — han ruller hurtigere og hurtigere væk fra centrum — hvorhen? ind i intet? ind i »den begejstrende fornemmelse af sin egen intethed«? — Nuvel! dette ville være den lige vej — til det gamle ideal? — Al videnskab (og på ingen måde kun astronomi, med hensyn til den ydmygende og forringende virkning af hvilken Kant har gjort en bemærkelsesværdig tilståelse, »den tilintetgør min egen vigtighed«), al videnskab, naturlig så vel som unaturlig — ved unaturlig mener jeg fornuftens selvkritik — sætter i dag sig for at tale mennesket ud af hans nuværende mening om sig selv, som om den mening havde været intet andet end et bizart stykke indbildning; du kunne gå så langt som at sige, at videnskaben finder sin særegne stolthed, sin særegne bitre form for stoisk ataraxia, i at bevare menneskets foragt for sig selv, denne tilstand, som det tog så meget besvær at frembringe, som menneskets endelige og mest alvorlige krav på selvanerkendelse (med rette, faktisk, for han, der foragter, er altid »en, der ikke har glemt, hvordan man påskønner«). Men involverer alt dette nogen virkelig anstrengelse for at modvirke det asketiske ideal? Foreslås det virkelig seriøst, at Kants sejr over den teologiske dogmatisme om »Gud«, »Sjæl«, »Frihed«, »Udødelighed« har skadet det ideal på nogen måde (som teologerne har forestillet sig, at det har været tilfældet i lang tid)? — Og i denne sammenhæng vedkommer det os ikke et eneste minut, om Kant selv havde til hensigt at fuldbyrde noget sådant. Det er sikkert, at fra Kants tid spiller hver type transcendentalist et vindende spil — de er emanciperet fra teologerne; hvilken lykke! — han har afsløret for dem den hemmelige kunst, hvorved de nu kan forfølge deres »hjertes ønske« på eget ansvar og med al videnskabens respektabilitet. Tilsvarende, hvem kan brokke sig over agnostikerne, tilbedere, som de er, af det ukendte og det absolutte mysterium, hvis de nu tilbeder selve deres spørgsmål som Gud? (Xaver Doudan taler et eller andet sted om den hærgen, som l'habitude d'admirer l'inintelligible au lieu de rester tout simplement dans l'inconnu har frembragt — de gamle, mener han, må have været fritaget for den hærgen.) Forudsat at alt, »kendt« af mennesket, undlader at tilfredsstille hans ønsker, og tværtimod modsiger og forfærder dem, hvilken guddommelig udvej fra alt dette at kunne lede efter ansvaret, ikke i det »ønskende«, men i det »vidende«! — »Der er ingen erkendelse. Følgelig — er der en Gud«; hvilken roman elegantia syllogismi! hvilken triumf for det asketiske ideal!

danishChanges.before: 26. Eller viser måske hele den moderne historie i sin opførsel større tillid til livet, større tillid til sine idealer? Dens højeste prætention er nu at være et spejl; den forkaster al teleologi; den vil ikke længere »bevise«; den vrager at spille dommer, og viser derved sin gode smag — den hævder lige så lidt, som den benægter, den fastlægger, den »beskriver«. Alt dette er i høj grad asketisk, men på samme tid er det i langt højere grad nihilistisk; gør ingen fejl om dette! Du ser hos historikeren et dystert, hårdt, men beslutsomt blik — et øje, der ser ud, som en isoleret nordpolsforsker ser ud (måske for ikke at se indad, for ikke at se tilbage?) — der er sne — her er livet bragt til tavshed, de sidste krager, der skvadrer her, kaldes »hvorhen?« »Forfængelighed«, »Nada« — her blomstrer og vokser intet mere, højst metapolitikken i Skt. Petersborg og Tolstojs »medlidenhed«. Men hvad angår denne anden skole af historikere, en måske endnu mere »moderne« skole, en sanselig og lasciv skole, der skotter til livet og det asketiske ideal med samme glød, der bruger ordet »kunstner« som en handske, og i dag har etableret et »hjørne« for sig selv i al den ros, der gives til kontemplationen; åh, hvilken tørst vækker disse søde intellektuelle endda til askese og vinterlandskaber! Nej! Djævelen tage disse »kontemplative« folk! Hvor meget hellere ville jeg vandre med disse historiske nihilister gennem den dystreste, grå, kolde tåge! — nej, jeg vil ikke have noget imod at lytte (forudsat at jeg må vælge) til en, der er fuldstændig uhistorisk og antihistorisk (en mand, som Dühring for eksempel, over hvis perioder en hidtil genertet og uudtalt art af »smukke sjæle« er vokset beruset i nutidens Tyskland, species anarchistica blandt det dannede proletariat). De »kontemplative« er hundrede gange værre — jeg har aldrig kendt noget, der frembragte så intens kvalme som en af disse »objektive« lærestole, en af disse parfumerede pyntedukker af historie, en ting halvt præst, halvt satyr (Renan parfum), der røber ved den høje, skrillende falset af sin bifald, hvad han mangler, og hvor han mangler det, der røber, hvor i dette tilfælde Skæbnerne har anvendt deres frygtelige saks, ak! på en alt for kirurgisk måde! Dette er usmageligt for mig og irriterer min tålmodighed; lad ham være tålmodig ved sådanne syn, der intet har at miste derved — et sådant syn raser mig, sådanne tilskuere forbittrer mig mod »spillet«, endnu mere end selve spillet (historien selv, du forstår); anakreontiske stemninger kommer umærkeligt over mig. Denne natur, der gav studen sit horn, løven sin χάσμ' ὀδόντων, til hvilket formål gav naturen mig min fod? — Til at sparke, ved Skt. Anakreon, og ikke blot til at løbe væk! Til at trampe på alle de ormstukne »lærestole«, de fejhede kontemplatorer, historiens lascive eunukker, asketiske idealers flirter, magtesløshedens retfærdige hyklere! Al ærefrygt fra min side til det asketiske ideal, for så vidt det er ærefuldt! Så længe det tror på sig selv og ikke spiller os pranks! Men jeg kan ikke lide alle disse koketterende biller, der har en umættelig ærgerrighed efter at lugte af det uendelige, indtil til sidst det uendelige lugter af biller; jeg kan ikke lide de hvidkalkede grave med deres scenske gengivelse af livet; jeg kan ikke lide de trætte og udbrændte, der svøber sig i visdom og ser »objektive« ud; jeg kan ikke lide agitatorerne, der er klædt ud som helte, som skjuler deres dukkehoveder bag et ideals stalking-hest; jeg kan ikke lide de ærgerrige kunstnere, der gerne vil spille asketen og præsten, og som i bunden ikke er andet end tragiske klovne; jeg kan ikke lide, igen, disse nyeste idealismespekulanter, antisemitterne, der i dag ruller deres øjne på den patenterede kristen-arisk-mand-af-ære-måde og ved en misbrug af moralistiske holdninger og agitationsfif, så billige at de udtømmer enhver tålmodighed, stræber efter at ophidse alle blokhovederne i pøblen (den uvægerlige succes for enhver form for intellektuelt charlataneri i nutidens Tyskland hænger sammen med den næsten ubestridelige og allerede ganske håndgribelige forarmelse af det tyske sind, hvis årsag jeg ser i en alt for ekskluderende diæt af aviser, politik, øl og wagnersk musik, for ikke at glemme denne diæts forudsætning, den nationale eksklusivitet og forfængelighed, det stærke, men snævre princip »Tyskland, Tyskland over alt« og endelig de »moderne idéers« paralysis agitans). Europa er i dag frem for alt rigt og opfindsomt i ophidselsesmidler; det har tilsyneladende ingen mere skrigende nødvendighed end stimulantia og alkohol. Heraf den enorme forfalskning af idealer, disse ildfuldeste ånder af sindet; heraf også den frastødende, ildelugtende, mensvorne, pseudoalkoholiske luft overalt. Jeg ville gerne vide, hvor mange skibsladninger imitation-idealisme, hvor mange heltekostumer og opblæste klap-trap, hvor mange tønder forsødet medlidenhedslikør (firma: la religion de la souffrance), hvor mange krykker af retfærdig harme til hjælp for disse fladfodede intellekter, hvor mange komedianter af det kristne moralske ideal i dag skulle eksporteres fra Europa for at sætte dets luft i stand til at lugte rent igen. Det er åbenbart, at der med hensyn til denne overproduktion ligger en ny handelsmulighed åben; det er åbenbart, at der er en ny forretning at lave i små idealidoler og lydige »idealister« — gå ikke hen over dette tip! Hvem har tilstrækkeligt mod? Vi har i vores hænder muligheden for at idealisere hele jorden. Men hvad taler jeg om mod? vi har kun brug for én ting her — en hånd, en fri, en meget fri hånd.

26. Eller viser måske hele den moderne historieskrivning i sin fremtræden større tillid til livet, større tillid til sine idealer? Dens højeste prætention er nu at være et spejl; den forkaster al teleologi; den vil ikke længere »bevise«; den afviser at spille dommer, og viser derved sin gode smag — den hævder lige så lidt, som den benægter, den fastlægger, den »beskriver«. Alt dette er i høj grad asketisk, men på samme tid er det i langt højere grad nihilistisk; tag ikke fejl! Du ser hos historikeren et dystert, hårdt, men beslutsomt blik — et øje, der ser ud, som en isoleret nordpolsforsker ser ud (måske for ikke at se indad, for ikke at se tilbage?) — der er sne — her er livet bragt til tavshed, de sidste krager, der skvadrer her, kaldes »hvorhen?« »Forgæves«, »Nada« — her blomstrer og vokser intet mere, højst metapolitikken i Skt. Petersborg og Tolstojs »medlidenhed«. Men hvad angår denne anden skole af historikere, en måske endnu mere »moderne« skole, en sanselig og lasciv skole, der skotter til livet og det asketiske ideal med samme glød, der bruger ordet »kunstner« som en handske, og i dag har etableret et »hjørne« for sig selv i al den ros, der gives til kontemplationen; åh, hvilken tørst vækker disse søde intellektuelle efter selv askese og vinterlandskaber! Nej! Djævelen tage disse »kontemplative« folk! Hvor meget hellere ville jeg vandre med disse historiske nihilister gennem den dystreste, grå, kolde tåge! — nej, jeg vil ikke have noget imod at lytte (forudsat at jeg må vælge) til en, der er fuldstændig uhistorisk og antihistorisk (en mand, som Dühring for eksempel, hvis sætningsperioder en hidtil sky og uerkendt art af »smukke sjæle« i nutidens Tyskland har beruset sig i, species anarchistica blandt det dannede proletariat). De »kontemplative« er hundrede gange værre — jeg har aldrig kendt noget, der frembragte så intens kvalme som en af disse »objektive« lærestole[6], en af disse parfumerede pyntedukker af historie, en ting halvt præst, halvt satyr (Renan parfum), der røber ved den høje, skingre falset i sit bifald, hvad han mangler, og hvor han mangler det, der røber, hvor i dette tilfælde Skæbnerne har anvendt deres frygtelige saks, ak! på en alt for kirurgisk måde! Dette er usmageligt for mig og sætter min tålmodighed på prøve; lad ham være tålmodig ved sådanne syn, der intet har at miste derved — et sådant syn gør mig rasende, sådanne tilskuere forbittrer mig mod »spillet«, endnu mere end selve spillet (historien selv, du forstår); anakreontiske stemninger kommer umærkeligt over mig. Denne natur, der gav studen sit horn, løven sin χάσμ' ὀδόντων, til hvilket formål gav naturen mig min fod? — Til at sparke, ved Skt. Anakreon, og ikke blot til at løbe væk! Til at trampe på alle de ormstukne »lærestole«, de feje betragtere, historiens lascive eunukker, dem, der flirter med asketiske idealer, magtesløshedens retfærdige hyklere! Al ærefrygt fra min side til det asketiske ideal, for så vidt det er ærefuldt! Så længe det tror på sig selv og ikke driver gæk med os! Men jeg kan ikke lide alle disse koketterende væggelus, der har en umættelig ærgerrighed efter at lugte af det uendelige, indtil til sidst det uendelige lugter af væggelus; jeg kan ikke lide de hvidkalkede grave med deres sceniske gengivelse af livet; jeg kan ikke lide de trætte og udbrændte, der svøber sig i visdom og ser »objektive« ud; jeg kan ikke lide agitatorerne, der er klædt ud som helte, som skjuler deres dukkehoveder bag et ideal som skalkeskjul; jeg kan ikke lide de ærgerrige kunstnere, der gerne vil spille asketen og præsten, og som i grunden ikke er andet end tragiske klovne; jeg kan ikke lide, igen, disse nyeste idealismespekulanter, antisemitterne, der i dag ruller deres øjne på deres velkendte manér som kristne, ariske hædersmænd og ved misbrug af moralistiske holdninger og agitationsfif, så billige, at de opbruger enhver tålmodighed, stræber efter at ophidse alle fæhovederne i pøblen (den uvægerlige succes for enhver form for intellektuelt charlataneri i nutidens Tyskland hænger sammen med den næsten ubestridelige og allerede ganske håndgribelige forarmelse af det tyske sind, hvis årsag jeg ser i en alt for ensidig kost af aviser, politik, øl og wagnersk musik, for ikke at glemme denne diæts forudsætning, den nationale eksklusivitet og forfængelighed, det stærke, men snævre princip »Tyskland, Tyskland over alt«[7] og endelig de »moderne idéers« paralysis agitans). Europa er i dag frem for alt rigt og opfindsomt i ophidselsesmidler; det har tilsyneladende intet mere skrigende behov end stimulantia og alkohol. Heraf den enorme forfalskning af idealer, disse åndens stærkeste spirituosa; heraf også den frastødende, ildelugtende, mensvorne, pseudoalkoholiske luft overalt. Jeg ville gerne vide, hvor mange skibsladninger efterlignet idealisme, hvor mange heltekostumer og opblæst ordskvalder, hvor mange tønder forsødet medlidenhedslikør (firma: la religion de la souffrance), hvor mange krykker af retfærdig harme til hjælp for disse fladfodede intellekter, hvor mange komedianter, der spiller det kristne moralideal i dag skulle eksporteres fra Europa for at luften her kunne dufte rent igen. Det er åbenbart, at der med hensyn til denne overproduktion ligger en ny handelsmulighed åben; det er åbenbart, at der er en ny forretning at lave i små idealidoler og lydige »idealister« — lad ikke dette vink gå upåagtet hen! Hvem har tilstrækkeligt mod? Vi har i vores hænder muligheden for at idealisere hele jorden. Men hvad taler jeg om mod? vi har kun brug for én ting her — en hånd, en fri, en meget fri hånd.

danishChanges.before: 27. Nok! nok! lad os forlade disse moderne sinds kuriositeter og kompleksiteter, der vækker lige så megen latter som afsky. Vores problem kan bestemt klare sig uden dem, problemet om det asketiske ideals betydning — hvad har det at gøre med i går eller i dag? Disse ting skal behandles af mig mere grundigt og strengt i en anden sammenhæng (under titlen »Et Bidrag til Historien om Europæisk Nihilisme«, jeg henviser til dette til et værk, jeg forbereder: Viljen til Magt, et Forsøg på en Omvurdering af Alle Værdier). Den eneste grund til, at jeg kommer til at hentyde til det her, er denne: det asketiske ideal har til tider, selv i den mest intellektuelle sfære, kun én virkelig slags fjender og skadevoldere: disse er dette ideals komedianter — for de vækker mistro. Overalt ellers, hvor sindet er på arbejde alvorligt, kraftfuldt og uden forfalskning, undværer det nu helt et ideal (det folkelige udtryk for denne afholdenhed er »ateisme«) — med undtagelse af viljen til sandhed. Men denne vilje, denne rest af et ideal, er, om du vil tro mig, selve dette ideal i dets strengeste og mest snedige formulering, esoterisk gennem og gennem, strippet for alle udposter, og følgelig ikke så meget dets rest som dets kerne. Ubetinget ærlig ateisme (og dens luft alene indånder vi, vi, denne tidsalders mest intellektuelle mænd) er ikke modsat dette ideal, i den udstrækning det synes at være; den er snarere en af de endelige faser af dets udvikling, en af dets syllogismer og stykker af iboende logik — den er den ærefrygtindgydende katastrofe af en to tusind år gammel træning i sandhed, der til sidst forbyder sig selv løgnen om troen på Gud. (Samme udviklingsforløb i Indien — ganske uafhængigt og følgelig af en eller anden demonstrativ værdi — det samme ideal, der drev til samme konklusion, det afgørende punkt nået fem hundrede år før den europæiske æra, eller mere præcist på Buddhas tid — det startede i Sankhyam-filosofien, og så blev dette popularieret gennem Buddha og lavet til en religion.)

danishChanges.before: Hvad har, stiller jeg spørgsmålet med al strenghed, virkelig triumferet over den kristne Gud? Svaret står i min Den Glade Videnskab, aforisme 357: »den kristne moral selv, idéen om sandhed, taget som den blev med stigende alvor, den kristne samvittigheds skriftefader-subtilitet oversat og sublimeret til den videnskabelige samvittighed, til intellektuel renhed for enhver pris. At betragte Naturen, som om den var et bevis på Guds godhed og varetægt; at fortolke historien til ære for en guddommelig fornuft, som et konstant bevis på en moralsk orden i verden og en moralsk teleologi; at forklare vore egne personlige erfaringer, som fromme mænd længe har forklaret dem, som om hvert arrangement, hvert nik, hver enkelt ting var opfundet og udsendt af kærlighed til sjælens frelse; alt dette er nu afskaffet, alt dette har samvittigheden imod sig og betragtes af enhver finere samvittighed som vanærende, ubehageligt, som løgn, feminisme, svaghed, fejhed — ved hjælp af denne strenghed, om ved hjælp af noget overhovedet, er vi sandelig gode europæere og arvinger til Europas længste og modigste selvbeherskelse.«... Alle store ting går til grunde af sig selv, af en selvopløsende handling: således vil livets lov, den nødvendige »selvbeherskelses« lov selv i livets essens — altid er lovgiveren til sidst udsat for råbet, »patere legem quam ipse tulisti«; på denne måde gik kristendommen til grunde som dogma, gennem sin egen moral; på denne måde må kristendommen i dag igen gå til grunde som moral — vi står på tærsklen til denne begivenhed. Efter at den kristne sandfærdighed har draget den ene slutning efter den anden, drager den endelig sin stærkeste slutning, sin slutning mod sig selv; dette sker imidlertid, når den stiller spørgsmålet, »hvad betyder hver vilje til sandhed?« Og her berører jeg igen mit problem, vores problem, mine ukendte venner (for jeg kender endnu ingen venner): hvilken mening har hele vores væren, hvis det ikke betyder, at i vore egne selv er denne vilje til sandhed kommet til sin egen bevidsthed som et problem? — Ved kraft af denne opnåelse af selvbevidsthed fra sandhedsviljens side går moralen herefter — der er ingen tvivl om det — i stykker: dette er det store hundredeakts skuespil, der er forbeholdt de næste to århundreder af Europa, det mest frygtelige, det mest mysteriøse og måske også det mest håbefulde af alle skuespil.

danishChanges.before: 28. Hvis man undtager det asketiske ideal, havde mennesket, dyremennesket, ingen mening. Hans eksistens på jorden indeholdt intet mål; »Hvad er overhovedet menneskets formål?« var et spørgsmål uden svar; viljen til mennesket og verden manglede; bag hver stor menneskelig skæbne lød som et omkvæd et endnu større »Forfængelighed!« Det asketiske ideal betyder simpelthen dette: at der manglede noget, at et uhyre tomrum omringede mennesket — han vidste ikke, hvordan han skulle retfærdiggøre sig selv, forklare sig selv, bekræfte sig selv, han led under problemet om sin egen mening. Han led også på andre måder, han var i hovedsagen et sygt dyr; men hans problem var ikke selve lidelsen, men manglen på et svar på dette skrigende spørgsmål, »Med hvilket formål lider vi?« Mennesket, det modigste dyr og det mest hærdet til lidelse, forkaster ikke lidelsen i sig selv: han vil den, han søger den endda, forudsat at der vises ham en mening med den, et formål med lidelsen. Ikke lidelsen, men lidelsens meningsløshed var den forbandelse, der indtil da havde ligget udbredt over menneskeheden — og det asketiske ideal gav den en mening! Det var indtil da den eneste mening; men en hvilken som helst mening er bedre end ingen mening; det asketiske ideal var i den henseende »faute de mieux« par excellence, der eksisterede på den tid. I dette ideal fandt lidelsen en forklaring; det uhyre hul syntes fyldt; døren til al selvmorderisk nihilisme blev lukket. Forklaringen — der er ingen tvivl om det — bragte i sit kølvand ny lidelse, dybere, mere gennemtrængende, mere giftig, gnavende mere brutalt ind i livet: den bragte al lidelse under skyldens perspektiv; men trods alt dette — blev mennesket reddet derved, han havde en mening, og var fra nu af ikke længere som et blad i vinden, en boldspiller for tilfældet, for meningsløshed, han kunne nu »ville« noget — fuldstændig ligegyldigt til hvilket mål, til hvilket formål, med hvilke midler han ønskede: viljen selv blev reddet. Det er fuldstændig umuligt at forklæde, hvad faktisk er gjort klart af enhver fuldstændig vilje, der har taget sin retning fra det asketiske ideal: dette had til det menneskelige og endda mere til det dyriske, og endnu mere til det materielle, denne rædsel for sanserne, for selve fornuften, denne frygt for lykke og skønhed, dette ønske om at komme væk fra al illusion, forandring, vækst, død, ønsken og selv begæring — alt dette betyder — lad os have modet til at gribe det — en vilje til intethed, en vilje modsat livet, en forkastelse af de mest fundamentale livsbetingelser, men det er og forbliver en vilje! — og at sige til sidst det, jeg sagde i begyndelsen — mennesket vil hellere ville intetheden end slet ikke ville.

englishChanges.before: 3. I have a scrupulosity peculiar to myself, which I confess reluctantly — it concerns morality. It showed itself in my life so early, so spontaneously, so persistently, and in such keen opposition to environment, epoch, precedent and ancestry, that I would almost be entitled to call it my "â priori." So my curiosity and my suspicion were early bound to halt at the question of what the origin of our "Good" and our "Evil" actually was. Indeed, at the boyish age of thirteen the problem of the origin of Evil already haunted me. At an age "when games and God divide one's heart," I devoted my first childish attempt at the literary game, my first philosophic essay, to that problem. As for my childish solution, well, I quite properly gave the honor to God and made him the father of evil. Did my own "â priori" demand that solution from me? That new, immoral, or at least "amoral" "â priori," and the "categorical imperative" which was its voice (but oh! how hostile to the Kantian article, and how pregnant with problems!), has had more and more of my attention since then, and indeed more than attention. Fortunately I soon learned to separate theological from moral prejudices, and I gave up looking for a supernatural origin of evil. A certain amount of historical and philological education, to say nothing of an innate faculty of psychological discrimination par excellence, almost immediately transformed my original problem into the following one: Under what conditions did Man invent for himself those judgments of values, "Good" and "Evil"? And what intrinsic value do they have in themselves? Have they so far hindered or advanced human well-being? Are they a symptom of the distress, impoverishment and degeneration of Human Life? Or, conversely, do the fullness, the strength and the will of Life, its courage, its self-confidence, its future, show themselves in them? On this point I found and hazarded in my mind the most diverse answers. I established distinctions among periods, peoples and castes, and I became a specialist in my problem. From my answers grew new questions, new investigations, new conjectures, new probabilities, until at last I had a land of my own and a soil of my own, a whole secret world growing and flowering, like hidden gardens whose existence no one could have an inkling of. Oh, how happy we are, we finders of knowledge, provided that we know how to keep silent long enough.
englishChanges.after: 3. I have a scrupulosity peculiar to myself, which I confess reluctantly — it concerns morality. It showed itself in my life so early, so spontaneously, so persistently, and in such keen opposition to environment, age, precedent and ancestry, that I would almost be entitled to call it my "â priori." So my curiosity and my suspicion were early bound to halt at the question of what the origin of our "Good" and our "Evil" actually was. Indeed, at the boyish age of thirteen the problem of the origin of Evil already haunted me. At an age "when games and God divide one's heart," I devoted my first childish attempt at the literary game, my first philosophic essay, to that problem. As for my childish solution, well, I quite properly gave the honor to God and made him the father of evil. Did my own "â priori" demand that solution from me? That new, immoral, or at least "amoral" "â priori," and the "categorical imperative" which was its voice (but oh! how hostile to the Kantian article, and how pregnant with problems!), has had more and more of my attention since then, and indeed more than attention. Fortunately I soon learned to separate theological from moral prejudices, and I gave up looking for a supernatural origin of evil. A certain amount of historical and philological education, to say nothing of an innate faculty of psychological discrimination par excellence, almost immediately transformed my original problem into the following one: Under what conditions did Man invent for himself those judgments of values, "Good" and "Evil"? englishChanges.before: 4. I owe my first impulse to publish some of my hypotheses on the origin of morality to a clear, well-written and even precocious little book. In it a perverse and vicious kind of moral philosophy (your real English kind) was presented to me definitely for the first time. It attracted me with that magnetic attraction which belongs to whatever is diametrically opposed and antithetical to one's own ideas. The title of the book was The Origin of the Moral Emotions; its author was Dr. Paul Rée; the year of its appearance was 1877. I may almost say that I have never read anything in which every single dogma and conclusion called forth from me so emphatic a negation as in that book — though it was a negation tainted by either pique or intolerance. In the works on which I was then working I therefore referred, in season and out of season, to the arguments of that book. I did not mean to refute them — for what have I to do with mere refutations? As is natural to a positive mind, I substituted a more probable theory for an improbable one, and occasionally, no doubt, one philosophic error for another. In that early period I gave, as I have said, the first public expression to the theories of origin to which these essays are devoted. I did it with a clumsiness that I was the last to conceal from myself, for I was still cramped, still without a special language for these special subjects, and still frequently liable to relapse and vacillation. For details, compare what I say in Human, all-too-Human, part i., about the parallel early history of Good and Evil, Aph. 45 (namely, their origin from the castes of the aristocrats and the slaves); similarly, Aph. 136 et seq., on the birth and value of ascetic morality; similarly, Aphs. 96, 99, vol. ii., Aph. 89, on the Morality of Custom, that far older and more original kind of morality which is toto cœlo different from the altruistic ethics (in which Dr. Rée, like all the English moral philosophers, sees the ethical "Thing-in-itself"); finally, Aph. 92. Similarly, Aph. 26 in Human, all-too-Human, part ii., and Aph. 112, the Dawn of Day, on the origin of Justice as a balance between persons of approximately equal power (equilibrium as the hypothesis of all contract, and consequently of all law); similarly, on the origin of Punishment, Human, all-too-Human, part ii., Aphs. 22, 23, on which point the deterrent object is neither essential nor original (as Dr. Rée thinks: rather this object is only imported, under certain definite conditions, and always as something extra and additional).

englishChanges.before: 5. In reality I had set my heart at that time on something much more important than the theories, mine or others', about the origin of morality (or, more precisely, the real function of these theories, from my view, was to point to an end to which they were one means among many). The issue for me was the value of morality, and on that subject I had to place myself in a state of abstraction in which I was almost alone with my great teacher Schopenhauer, to whom that book, with all its passion and inherent contradiction (for that book also was a polemic), turned for present help as though he were still alive. The issue was, strangely enough, the value of the "un-egoistic" instincts, the instincts of pity, self-denial and self-sacrifice, which Schopenhauer had so persistently painted in golden colors, deified and etherealized, that eventually they seemed to him, as it were, high and dry, "intrinsic values in themselves," on the strength of which he uttered his own negation, both to Life and to himself. But against these very instincts a more and more fundamental mistrust voiced itself in my soul, a skepticism that dug ever deeper and deeper. In this very instinct I saw the great danger of mankind, its most sublime temptation and seduction — seduction to what? to nothingness? In these very instincts I saw the beginning of the end, stability, the exhaustion that gazes backwards, the will turning against Life, the last illness announcing itself with its own mincing melancholy. I realized that the morality of pity, which spread wider and wider and whose grip infected even philosophers with its disease, was the most sinister symptom of our modern European civilization. I realized that it was the route along which that civilization slid on its way to — a new Buddhism? — a European Buddhism? — Nihilism? This exaggerated estimation in which modern philosophers have held pity is quite a new phenomenon: up to that time philosophers were absolutely unanimous about the worthlessness of pity. I need only mention Plato, Spinoza, La Rochefoucauld and Kant — four minds as different from each other as is possible, but united on one point: their contempt of pity.

englishChanges.before: 6. This problem of the value of pity and of the pity-morality (I am an opponent of the modern infamous emasculation of our emotions) seems at first blush a mere isolated problem, a note of interrogation standing by itself. But whoever once halts at this problem and learns how to put questions will experience what I experienced. A new and immense vista unfolds before him, a sense of potentiality seizes him like a vertigo, every species of doubt, mistrust and fear springs up, the belief in morality, nay, in all morality, totters — and finally a new demand voices itself. Let us speak out this new demand: we need a critique of moral values, and the value of these values is to be called into question for the first time. For this we need a knowledge of the conditions and circumstances out of which these values grew, under which they evolved and became distorted (morality as a result, as a symptom, as a mask, as Tartuffism, as disease, as a misunderstanding; but also morality as a cause, as a remedy, as a stimulant, as a fetter, as a drug). We need it all the more because such a knowledge has neither existed until now nor is even now generally desired. The value of these "values" was taken for granted as an indisputable fact, beyond all question. No one has shown the faintest doubt or hesitation, until now, in judging the "good man" to be of higher value than the "evil man" — higher value specifically for human progress, utility and prosperity generally, not forgetting the future. What? Suppose the converse were the truth! What? Suppose there lurked in the "good man" a symptom of retrogression, such as a danger, a temptation, a poison, a narcotic, by means of which the present battened on the future! More comfortable and less risky perhaps than its opposite, but also pettier, meaner! So that morality would really be saddled with the guilt, if the maximum potentiality of the power and splendor of the human species were never to be attained? So that really morality would be the danger of dangers?

englishChanges.before: 7. Enough: after this vista had disclosed itself to me, I had reason to search for learned, bold and industrious colleagues (I am doing it even to this very day). It means traversing the immense, distant and completely unexplored land of morality with new clamorous questions and at the same time with new eyes — a morality which has actually existed and been actually lived! And is this not practically equivalent to first discovering that land? If I thought, among others, of the aforesaid Dr. Rée in this context, I did so because I had no doubt that the very nature of his questions would compel him to have recourse to a truer method in order to obtain his answers. Have I deceived myself on that score? At all events I wished to give a better direction of vision to an eye of such keenness and such impartiality. I wished to direct him to the real history of morality, and to warn him, while there was yet time, against a world of English theories that culminated in the blue vacuum of heaven. Other colors, of course, rise immediately to one's mind as being a hundred times more potent than blue for a genealogy of morals: for instance, gray, by which I mean authentic facts capable of definite proof and actually existing — or, to put it shortly, the whole of that long hieroglyphic script (so hard to decipher) of the past history of human morals. This script was unknown to Dr. Rée; but he had read Darwin. And so in his philosophy the Darwinian beast and that pink of modernity, the demure weakling and dilettante who "bites no longer," shake hands politely, in a fashion that is at least instructive. The latter wears a certain facial expression of refined and good-humored indolence, tinged with a touch of pessimism and exhaustion, as if it really did not pay to take all these things — I mean moral problems — so seriously. I, on the other hand, think that there are no subjects which pay better for being taken seriously; part of this payment is that perhaps eventually they admit of being taken gaily. This gaiety, or, to use my own language, this joyful wisdom, is indeed a payment — a payment for a protracted, brave, laborious and burrowing seriousness, which, it goes without saying, is the attribute of but a few. But on the day when we say from the fullness of our hearts, "Forward! our old morality too is fit material for Comedy," we shall have discovered a new plot and a new possibility for the Dionysian drama entitled The Soul's Fate — and he will speedily make use of it, one can safely wager, he, the great ancient eternal dramatist of the comedy of our existence.

englishChanges.before: 8. If this writing is obscure to anyone and jars on his ears, I do not think that I am necessarily to blame. It is clear enough on the hypothesis I presuppose, namely that the reader has first read my previous writings and has not grudged them a certain amount of trouble: it is not, indeed, a simple matter to get at their essence. Take, for instance, my Zarathustra. I allow no one to pass as knowing that book unless every single word in it has at some time wounded him profoundly and at some time enchanted him profoundly. Then, and not till then, can he enjoy the privilege of reverently sharing in the halcyon element from which that work is born, in its sunny brilliance, its distance, its spaciousness, its certainty. In other cases the aphoristic form produces difficulty, but this is only because the form is treated too casually. An aphorism properly coined and cast into its final mold is far from being "deciphered" as soon as it has been read; on the contrary, that is when it first requires to be expounded — and for that an art of exposition is of course necessary. The third essay in this book provides an example of what I call exposition in such cases: an aphorism is prefixed to that essay, and the essay itself is its commentary. One quality is certainly essential in order to practise reading as an art, and it has nowadays been best forgotten — that is why it will take some time yet for my writings to become readable. It is a quality for which one must be a cow, and under no circumstances a modern man! — rumination.

englishChanges.before: 2. All honor, then, to the noble spirits who would gladly dominate these historians of morality. But it is certainly a pity that they themselves lack the historical sense, and that all the beneficent spirits of history have deserted them. The whole train of their thought runs, as it always did with old-fashioned philosophers, along thoroughly unhistorical lines; there is no doubt of this. The crass ineptitude of their genealogy of morals shows at once when the question is the origin of the idea and judgment of "good." "Originally," so runs their decree, "man praised altruistic acts and called them 'good' from the standpoint of those on whom they were conferred, that is, those to whom they were useful. Later the origin of this praise was forgotten, and altruistic acts, simply because they were habitually praised as good, also came to be felt as good, as though they contained some intrinsic goodness." The thing is obvious: this first derivation already contains all the typical and peculiar traits of the English psychologists. We have "utility," "forgetting," "habit," and finally "error," the whole assemblage forming the basis of a system of values, of which the higher man has until now been proud, as though it were a privilege of man in general. This pride must be brought low, this system of values must lose its value: is that achieved?

englishChanges.before: 6. Above all, this rule has no exception (though there are opportunities for exceptions): the idea of political superiority always resolves itself into the idea of psychological superiority, wherever the highest caste is also the priestly caste and, true to its general character, gives itself a title that specifically alludes to its priestly function. In these cases "clean" and "unclean" first confront each other as badges of class distinction, for instance, and here again a "good" and a "bad" develop in a sense that is no longer merely social. Moreover, one should take care not to take these ideas of "clean" and "unclean" too seriously, too broadly, or too symbolically. All the ideas of ancient man must rather be understood, in their early stages, as crude, coarse, physical and narrow to an almost inconceivable extent, and above all as essentially unsymbolical. The "clean man" is originally only a man who washes himself, who abstains from certain foods that lead to skin diseases, who does not sleep with the unclean women of the lower classes, who has a horror of blood — not more, not much more! On the other hand, the very nature of a priestly aristocracy shows why the opposed values should have been sharpened and intensified, so dangerously, at just such an early stage. It is through these opposed values that gulfs are cleft in the social plane which a veritable Achilles of free thought would shudder to cross. Such sacerdotal aristocracies carry a diseased taint from the outset, and so do the habits that prevail in such societies. Averse to action, these habits are a compound of introspection and explosive emotionalism, and out of them comes the introspective morbidity and neurasthenia that cling almost inevitably to all priests at all times. As for the remedy the priests themselves invented for this disease, the philosopher has no option but to say that its effects have proved a hundred times more dangerous than the disease it was supposed to cure. Humanity itself is still sick from the naïvetés of this priestly cure. Take, for instance, certain kinds of diet (abstention from flesh), fasts, sexual continence, flight into the wilderness (a kind of Weir-Mitchell isolation, though of course without that system of excessive feeding and fattening which is the most efficient antidote to all the hysteria of the ascetic ideal). Consider too the whole metaphysic of the priests, with its war on the senses, its enervation, its hair-splitting. Consider its self-hypnotism on the fakir and Brahman principles (it uses Brahman as a glass disc and obsession), and that climax, which we understand only too well, of an unusual satiety with its panacea of nothingness (or God: the demand for a unio mystica with God is the demand of the Buddhist for nothingness, Nirvana — and nothing else!). In sacerdotal societies everything is more dangerous: not merely cures and remedies, but also pride, revenge, cunning, exaltation, love, ambition, virtue, morbidity. Further, one can fairly say that man first becomes an interesting animal on the soil of this essentially dangerous form of human society, the sacerdotal form. In it the human soul has, in a higher sense, gained depth and become evil. And these are the two fundamental ways in which man has shown himself superior to every other animal until now.

englishChanges.before: 7. The reader will already have guessed how easily the priestly mode of valuation can branch off from the knightly aristocratic mode and then grow into its very antithesis. The opposition gets a special impetus whenever the priestly and warrior castes confront each other in mutual jealousy and cannot agree over the prize. The knightly-aristocratic "values" rest on a careful cult of the physical, on a flowering, rich and even effervescing health that goes well beyond what is needed to maintain life, and on war, adventure, the chase, the dance, the tourney — on everything, in fact, that belongs to strong, free and joyous action. The priestly-aristocratic mode of valuation rests, as we have seen, on other hypotheses: war is bad enough for this class! Yet the priests are, as everyone knows, the worst enemies. Why? Because they are the weakest. Their weakness makes their hate swell into a monstrous and sinister shape, the most crafty and most poisonous shape. The really great haters in the history of the world have always been priests, who are also the cleverest haters; set beside the cleverness of priestly revenge, every other cleverness is practically negligible. Human history would be far too fatuous without the cleverness that the weak have brought into it. Take at once the most important instance. Everything the world has done against the "aristocrats," the "mighty," the "masters," the "holders of power," is negligible beside what the Jews have done against those classes. The Jews, that priestly nation, eventually saw that the one way to get satisfaction from its enemies and tyrants was a radical transvaluation of values, which was at the same time an act of the cleverest revenge. Only a nation of priests could use this method, a nation of the most jealously nursed priestly revengefulness. It was the Jews who dared, with terrifying logic, to set against the aristocratic equation (good = aristocratic = beautiful = happy = loved by the gods) the contrary equation, and to hold on to it with the teeth of the most profound hatred (the hatred of weakness): "the wretched alone are the good; the poor, the weak, the lowly alone are the good; the suffering, the needy, the sick, the loathsome are the only ones who are pious, the only ones who are blessed, for them alone is salvation. But you, on the other hand, you aristocrats, you men of power, you are to all eternity the evil, the horrible, the covetous, the insatiate, the godless; eternally also shall you be the unblessed, the cursed, the damned!" We know who inherited the fruits of this Jewish transvaluation. Faced with the monstrous and inordinately fateful initiative the Jews took in this most fundamental of all declarations of war, I remember the passage I once wrote (Beyond Good and Evil, Aph. 195): that the revolt of the slaves in morals begins, in fact, with the Jews; that this revolt has behind it a history of two millennia, and has now only moved out of our sight because it has achieved victory.

englishChanges.before: 10. The revolt of the slaves in morals begins when resentment itself becomes creative and gives birth to values. This is a resentment felt by creatures who, denied the proper outlet of action, are forced to find their compensation in an imaginary revenge. While every aristocratic morality springs from a triumphant affirmation of its own demands, the slave morality says "no" from the very outset to what is "outside itself," "different from itself," and "not itself": and this "no" is its creative deed. This reversal of the valuing standpoint — this inevitable turn toward the objective instead of back toward the subjective — is typical of "resentment." The slave-morality needs an external and objective world as the condition of its existence; to use physiological terms, it needs objective stimuli in order to be capable of action at all. Its action is fundamentally a reaction. The contrary is the case with the aristocrat's system of values: it acts and grows spontaneously, and seeks its antithesis only in order to say a more grateful and exultant "yes" to itself. Its negative conception, "low," "vulgar," "bad," is merely a pale, late-born foil beside its positive and fundamental conception (saturated as it is with life and passion): "we aristocrats, we good ones, we beautiful ones, we happy ones."

englishChanges.before: 11. This man's method is the exact opposite of the aristocrat's. The aristocrat forms the root idea "good" spontaneously, straight out of himself, and only then, from that material, creates for himself a concept of "bad"! This aristocratic "bad" and that "evil" from the cauldron of unsatisfied hatred are two very different things. The first is an imitation, an "extra," an additional nuance; the second is the original, the beginning, the essential act in the making of a slave-morality. Both "bad" and "evil" have the same opposite, "good," yet how great a difference they mark! For the idea "good" is not the same in each. Ask rather: "Who is really evil, according to the morality of resentment?" The answer, in all sternness, is this: just the good man of the other morality, just the aristocrat, the powerful one, the ruler, but seen through the venomous eye of resentfulness and so given a new color, a new meaning, a new look. We would be the last to deny this. A man who got to know those "good" ones only as enemies learned at the same time not to know them only as "evil enemies." Yet these same men are bound so rigorously inter pares by convention, respect, custom, and gratitude, and still more by mutual vigilance and jealousy inter pares. Among themselves they find so many new ways of showing consideration, self-control, delicacy, loyalty, pride, and friendship. But toward whatever lies outside their circle (where the foreign element, a foreign country, begins) they are not much better than beasts of prey let loose. There they are free of all social control. In the wilderness they can vent, with impunity, the tension built up by being fenced in and shut up within the peace of society. They revert to the innocence of the beast-of-prey conscience, like jubilant monsters who may be coming from a ghastly bout of murder, arson, rape, and torture, with bravado and moral equanimity, as if it were merely some wild student's prank, fully convinced that the poets now have plenty to sing and celebrate. At the core of all these aristocratic races we cannot fail to recognize the beast of prey, the magnificent blond brute, greedily prowling for spoil and victory. This hidden core needed an outlet from time to time; the beast had to get loose again and return to the wilderness. The Roman, Arabic, German, and Japanese nobility, the Homeric heroes, the Scandinavian Vikings, all share this need. The aristocratic races left the idea "Barbarian" behind on every path they marched. Nay, a consciousness of this very barbarianism, and even a pride in it, shows itself in their highest civilization (for example, when Pericles tells his Athenians in the celebrated funeral oration, "Our audacity has forced a way over every land and sea, rearing everywhere imperishable memorials of itself for good and for evil"). The audacity of aristocratic races may be mad, absurd, and spasmodic in its expression; their enterprises may be incalculable and fantastic — Pericles sets in special relief and glory the ᾽ραθυμία of the Athenians, their nonchalance and contempt for safety, body, life, and comfort, their awful joy and intense delight in all destruction, in all the ecstasies of victory and cruelty — all these features crystallized, for those who suffered from them, into the picture of the "barbarian," of the "evil enemy," perhaps of the "Goth" and the "Vandal." Even now, the German meets a profound, icy mistrust as soon as he comes to power. That mistrust is still an aftermath of the inextinguishable horror with which Europe, for whole centuries, regarded the wrath of the blond Teuton beast (although there is scarcely a psychological, let alone a physical, relationship between the old Germans and ourselves). I once pointed out Hesiod's embarrassment when he conceived the series of social ages and tried to express them in gold, silver, and bronze. The Homeric world confronted him with a contradiction: an age magnificent indeed, but at the same time so awful and so violent. He could resolve it only by making two ages out of one and setting them one behind the other. First came the age of the heroes and demigods, as that world lived on in the memories of the aristocratic families, who found their own ancestors in it. Then came the bronze age, as that same age looked to the descendants of the oppressed, spoiled, ill-treated, exiled, and enslaved: an age of bronze, as I have said, hard, cold, terrible, without feelings and without conscience, crushing everything and spattering everything with blood. Suppose the now-accepted theory is true, that the whole essence of civilization is to train the beast of prey out of man and make of him a tame and civilized animal, a domesticated animal. Then we must undoubtedly regard as the real tools of civilization all those instincts of reaction and resentment, with whose help the aristocratic races, together with their ideals, were finally degraded and overpowered. That is not yet to say that the bearers of those tools also represented civilization. The opposite is not merely probable — nay, it is palpable today. These bearers of vindictive instincts that have to be bottled up, these descendants of all European and non-European slavery, especially of the pre-Aryan population — these people, I say, represent the decline of humanity! These "tools of civilization" are a disgrace to humanity, and in reality they count more as an argument against civilization, more as a reason to be suspicious of it. One may be quite justified in always fearing the blond beast at the core of every aristocratic race, and in staying on one's guard. But who would not a hundred times rather fear, while admiring, than be free of fear and be forever obsessed with the loathsome sight of the distorted, the dwarfed, the stunted, the envenomed? And is that not our fate? What makes us feel repulsion toward "man" today? — for we suffer from "man," there is no doubt about it. It is not fear. It is rather that we have nothing left to fear from men; that the worm "man" is in the foreground and swarms; that the "tame man," the wretched, mediocre, unedifying creature, has learned to consider himself a goal and a pinnacle, an inner meaning, a historic principle, a "higher man." Yes, and he has a certain right to do so, in so far as he feels that, set against that excess of deformity, disease, exhaustion, and effeteness whose odor is beginning to pollute present-day Europe, he at any rate has achieved a relative success; he at any rate still says "yes" to life.

englishChanges.before: 15. In the faith in what? In the love for what? In the hope of what? These weaklings! — they also, forsooth, wish to be the strong some time; there is no doubt about it, some time their kingdom also must come — "the kingdom of God" is their name for it, as has been mentioned: they are so meek in everything! Yet to experience that kingdom one has to live long, to live beyond death — yes, eternal life is necessary, so that one can make up forever for that earthly life "in faith," "in love," "in hope." Make up for what? Make up by what? Dante, it seems to me, made a crass mistake when, with awe-inspiring ingenuity, he placed the inscription "Me too made eternal love" over the gate of his hell. At any rate, the inscription "Me too made eternal hate" would have a much better right to stand over the gate of the Christian Paradise and its "eternal blessedness" — granted, of course, that a truth may rightly stand over the gate to a lie! For what is the blessedness of that Paradise? Possibly we could quickly guess it; but it is better to have it explicitly attested by an authority not to be disparaged in such matters, Thomas of Aquinas, the great teacher and saint. "Beati in regno celesti" he says, as gently as a lamb, "videbunt pœnas damnatorum, ut beatitudo illis magis complaceat." Or if we wish to hear a stronger tone, here is a word from the mouth of a triumphant father of the Church, who warned his disciples against the cruel ecstasies of the public spectacles — But why? Faith offers us much more, he says, de Spectac., c. 29 ss., something much stronger. Thanks to the redemption, joys of quite another kind are at our disposal; instead of athletes we have our martyrs; if we wish for blood, well, we have the blood of Christ — but what then awaits us on the day of his return, of his triumph. And then he goes on, this enraptured visionary: "at enim supersunt alia spectacula, ille ultimas et perpetuus judicii dies, ille nationibus insperatus, ille derisus, cum tanta sæculi vetustas et tot ejus nativitates uno igne haurientur. Quæ tunc spectaculi latitudo! Quid admirer! quid rideam! Ubigaudeam! Ubi exultem, spectans tot et tantos reges, qui in cœlum recepti nuntiabantur, cum ipso Jove et ipsis suis testibus in imis tenebris congemescentes! Item præsides" (the provincial governors) "persecutores dominici nominis sævioribus quam ipsi flammis sævierunt insultantibus contra Christianos liquescentes! Quos præterea sapientes illos philosophos coram discipulis suis una conflagrantibus erubescentes, quibus nihil ad deum pertinere suadebant, quibus animas aut nullas aut non in pristina corpora redituras affirmabant! Etiam poetas non ad Rhadamanti nec ad Minois, sed ad inopinati Christi tribunal palpitantes! Tunc magis tragœdi audiendi, magis scilicet vocales" (with louder tones and more violent shrieks) "in sua propria calamitate; tunc histriones cognoscendi, solutiores multo per ignem; tunc spectandus auriga in flammea rota totus rubens, tunc xystici contemplandi non in gymnasiis, sed in igne jaculati, nisi quod ne tunc quidem illos velim vivos, ut qui malim ad eos potius conspectum insatiabilem conferre, qui in dominum scevierunt. Hic est ille, dicam fabri aut quæstuariæ filius" (as the whole of the following shows, and in particular this well-known description of the mother of Jesus from the Talmud, Tertullian is from here on referring to the Jews), "sabbati destructor, Samarites et dæmonium habens. Hic est quem a Juda redemistis, hic est ille arundine et colaphis diverberatus, sputamentis de decoratus, felle et acete potatus. Hic est, quem clam discentes subripuerunt, ut resurrexisse dicatur vel hortulanus detraxit, ne lactucæ suæ frequentia commeantium laderentur. Ut talia species, ut talibus exultes, quis tibi prætor aut consul aut sacerdos de sua liberalitate prastabit? Et tamen hæc jam habemus quodammodo per fidem spiritu imaginante repræsentata. Ceterum qualia illa sunt, quæ nec oculus vidit nec auris audivit nec in cor hominis ascenderunt?" (I Cor. ii. 9.) "Credo circo et utraque cavea" (the first and fourth row, or, according to others, the comic and the tragic stage) "et omni studio gratiora." Per fidem: so it stands written.

englishChanges.before: Which of them has been victorious for the time being, Rome or Judæa? There is not a shadow of doubt. Just consider whom you bow down to even in Rome itself today, as though to the quintessence of all the highest values — and not only in Rome, but over almost half the world, wherever man has been tamed or is about to be tamed. You bow to three Jews, as we know, and one Jewess (Jesus of Nazareth, Peter the fisher, Paul the tent-maker, and the mother of the aforesaid Jesus, named Mary). This is very remarkable: Rome is undoubtedly defeated. At any rate, in the Renaissance there was a brilliantly sinister revival of the classical ideal, of the aristocratic valuation of all things. Rome herself, like a man waking from a trance, stirred under the weight of the new Judaized Rome built over her, which looked like an œcumenical synagogue and was called the "Church." But Judæa immediately triumphed again, thanks to that fundamentally popular (German and English) movement of revenge called the Reformation, and thanks also to its inevitable corollary, the restoration of the Church — which also restored the ancient graveyard peace of classical Rome. In the French Revolution Judæa again proved victorious over the classical ideal, in a sense even more crucial and more profound. The last political aristocracy in Europe, that of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century France, broke into pieces under the instincts of a resentful populace. The world had never heard a greater jubilation, a more uproarious enthusiasm. Yet in the midst of it the most monstrous and unexpected thing happened: the ancient ideal itself rose before the eyes and conscience of humanity with all its life and with unheard-of splendor. Against resentment's lying war-cry of the prerogative of the most, against the will to lowliness, abasement, and equalization, the will to a retrogression and twilight of humanity, there rang out once more, stronger, simpler, and more penetrating than ever, the terrible and enchanting counter-warcry of the prerogative of the few! Then, like a final signpost to other ways, Napoleon appeared, the most unique and violent anachronism that ever existed, and in him the incarnate problem of the aristocratic ideal in itself. Consider well what a problem it is: Napoleon, that synthesis of Monster and Superman.

englishChanges.before: 17. Was that the end of it? Was that greatest of all antitheses of ideals thereby put ad acta for all time? Or only postponed, postponed for a long time? May there not come a day when the old conflagration flares up again, far more awful and far more carefully prepared? Further! Should one not wish for that outcome with all one's strength? — will it oneself? demand it oneself? Whoever begins at this point, like my readers, to reflect and think further will find it hard to reach a quick conclusion. That is reason enough for me to conclude myself, taking it for granted that by now it has been sufficiently clear what I mean, exactly what I mean by that dangerous motto inscribed on the body of my last book: Beyond Good and Evil — which at any rate is not the same as "Beyond Good and Bad."

englishChanges.before: On the other hand, it is of course equally necessary to interest physiologists and doctors in these problems (the value of the valuations that have prevailed until now). Here the professional philosophers may be trusted to act as spokesmen and intermediaries, once they have fully managed to turn the relationship between philosophy and physiology and medicine, originally one of coldness and suspicion, into the friendliest and most fruitful reciprocity. In fact, every table of values, every "thou shalt" known to history and ethnology, first needs a physiological elucidation and interpretation, at any rate in preference to a psychological one; all of them equally call for a critique from medical science. The question "What is the value of this or that table of 'values' and morality?" will be asked from the most varied standpoints. The question "valuable for what?", for instance, can never be analyzed with enough nicety. Something that would obviously be valuable for giving a race the greatest possible powers of endurance (or for increasing its adaptability to a specific climate, or for preserving the greatest number) would be nowhere near as valuable if the aim were to develop a stronger species. In gauging values, the good of the majority and the good of the minority are opposed standpoints. We leave it to the naïveté of English biologists to regard the first as intrinsically superior. All the sciences must now pave the way for the future task of the philosopher, understood as this: he must solve the problem of value, he has to fix the hierarchy of values.

englishChanges.before: 2. All this is simply the long history of the origin of responsibility. The task of breeding an animal that can make promises includes, as we have already seen, a more immediate task as its condition and preliminary: first to make man to a certain extent necessitated, uniform, like among his like, regular and therefore calculable. What I have called the "morality of custom" (cp. Dawn of Day, Aphs. 9, 14, and 16) was an immense work: man's actual work on himself during the longest period of the human race, his whole prehistoric work. This work finds its meaning and its great justification (in spite of all its innate hardness, despotism, stupidity and idiocy) in this: with the help of the morality of customs and of social strait-waistcoats, man was made genuinely calculable. But suppose we stand at the end of this colossal process, at the point where the tree finally ripens its fruit and society and its morality of custom at last bring to light what they were only the means to. There we find, as the ripest fruit on its tree, the sovereign individual, who resembles only himself, who has got loose from the morality of custom: the autonomous "super-moral" individual (for "autonomous" and "moral" exclude each other) — in short, the man of the personal, long and independent will, who is able to promise. In him we find a proud consciousness, vibrating in every fibre, of what has at last been achieved and has come alive in him, a genuine consciousness of power and freedom, a feeling of human perfection in general. And this man who has grown to freedom, who is really able to promise, this lord of the free will, this sovereign — how can he fail to know how great his superiority is over everything that cannot bind itself by promises or be its own security, how great a trust, awe and reverence he awakens (he "deserves" all three), and that with this mastery over himself he is necessarily also given mastery over circumstances, over nature, over all creatures with shorter wills and less reliable characters? The "free" man, the owner of a long, unbreakable will, finds in this possession his standard of value. Looking out from himself upon others, he honors or he despises. Just as necessarily as he honors his peers, the strong and the reliable (those who can bind themselves by promises) — that is, everyone who promises like a sovereign, with difficulty, rarely and slowly, who is sparing with his trust but confers honor by the very act of trusting, who gives his word as something that can be relied on because he knows himself strong enough to keep it even in the teeth of disasters, even in the "teeth of fate" — so with equal necessity will he have the heel of his foot ready for the lean and empty jackasses who promise when they have no business to, and his rod of chastisement ready for the liar who already breaks his word at the very moment it is on his lips. The proud knowledge of the extraordinary privilege of responsibility, the consciousness of this rare freedom, of this power over himself and over fate, has sunk right down to his innermost depths and has become an instinct, a dominating instinct. What name will he give to it, to this dominating instinct, if he needs a word for it? There is no doubt about it: the sovereign man calls it his conscience.
