englishChanges.before: Have these current genealogists of morals ever allowed themselves even the vaguest notion, for instance, that the cardinal moral idea of "ought" originates in the very material idea of "owe"? Or that punishment developed as a retaliation absolutely independently of any prior assumption about the freedom or determination of the will? — And this to such an extent that a high degree of civilization was always necessary first, before the animal man could begin to make those much more primitive distinctions of "intentional," "negligent," "accidental," "responsible," and their contraries, and apply them in assessing punishment. That idea — "the wrong-doer deserves punishment because he might have acted otherwise" — is nowadays so cheap, obvious, natural and inevitable, and has had to serve as an illustration of how the sentiment of justice appeared on earth; yet in fact it is an exceedingly late, even refined, form of human judgment and inference, and to project it back to the beginning of the world is simply a clumsy violation of the principles of primitive psychology. Throughout the longest period of human history punishment was never based on the evil-doer's responsibility for his action, and was therefore not based on the assumption that only the guilty should be punished. On the contrary, punishment was inflicted for the same reason that parents punish their children even nowadays: out of anger at an injury suffered, an anger that vents itself mechanically on the author of the injury. But this anger is kept in bounds and modified by the idea that every injury has somewhere its equivalent price and can really be paid off, even if by means of pain to the author. Where has this ancient, deep-rooted and now perhaps ineradicable idea, the idea of an equivalence between injury and pain, drawn its strength? I have already revealed its origin: it lies in the contractual relationship between creditor and debtor, which is as old as the existence of legal rights at all, and which in its turn points back to the primary forms of purchase, sale, barter and trade.

englishChanges.before: 9. Measured always by the standard of antiquity (and this antiquity is present, or possible again, in every period), the community stands toward its members in that important and radical relationship of creditor to his "debtors." Man lives in a community and enjoys its advantages (and what advantages! we sometimes underestimate them nowadays). He lives protected and spared, in peace and trust, safe from certain injuries and enmities to which the man outside the community, the "peaceless" man, is exposed (a German understands the original meaning of "Elend" (êlend)). He is safe because he has bound himself by pledges and obligations to the community with regard to those very injuries and enmities. What happens when this is not the case? The community, the defrauded creditor, will get itself paid as well as it can; one can count on that. In this case the direct damage done by the offender is quite secondary. Quite apart from it, the criminal is above all a breaker, a breaker of his word and covenant to the whole, with regard to all the advantages and amenities of communal life in which up to then he had shared. The criminal is a "debtor" who not only fails to repay the advances and advantages given to him, but even sets out to attack his creditor. So in the future he is not only deprived, as is fair, of all these advantages and amenities; he is also reminded how important those advantages were. The wrath of the injured creditor, the community, throws him back into the wild and outlawed state from which he was protected until then. The community repudiates him, and now every kind of enmity can vent itself on him. At this stage of civilization, punishment is simply the copy, the mimicry, of the normal treatment of the hated, despised and conquered enemy, who is deprived not only of every right and protection but of every mercy. So we have the martial law and the triumphant festival of the væ victis! in all its mercilessness and cruelty. This shows why war itself (counting the sacrificial cult of war) has produced all the forms in which punishment has appeared in history.

englishChanges.before: 12. Let me say a little more on the origin and the end of punishment. These are two problems that are, or ought to be, kept separate, but unfortunately they are usually thrown together. And how have our moral genealogists gone about it until now? With their inveterate naïveté. They discover some "end" in punishment, such as revenge or deterrence, and then in all their innocence place this end at the beginning, as the causa fiendi of the punishment, and they have done the trick. But the last use that the "End in Law" should be put to is patching together a history of the origin of law. For any kind of history, perhaps no principle is more pregnant than this one. It is hard to master, yet it should be mastered down to the last detail: the origin of a thing's existence and its final utility, its practical application and its place in a system of ends, are toto cœlo opposed to each other. Whatever exists and prevails anywhere will always be given new purposes by a force superior to it, will be taken over afresh, and will be turned and transformed to new uses. All "happening" in the organic world consists of overpowering and dominating, and all overpowering and domination is a new interpretation and adjustment, which must obscure, or even wholly extinguish, the "meaning" and "end" that existed before. You may understand perfectly the utility of some physiological organ (or of a legal institution, a social custom, a political habit, a form in art or religious worship), and that does not in the least mean you understand its origin. Older men may find this uncomfortable and unpalatable, for people have always believed that to understand the final cause or the utility of a thing, a form, an institution, was to understand why it came into being. By this logic the eye was made to see and the hand was made to grasp, and so punishment too was supposed to have been invented in order to punish. But all ends and all utilities are only signs that a Will to Power has mastered some less powerful force and has stamped on it, out of its own self, the meaning of a function. By the same principle, the whole history of a "Thing," an organ, a custom, can be seen as a continuous "sign-chain" of ever new interpretations and adjustments. Their causes need not be connected with one another at all; sometimes they simply follow and alternate by chance. In the same way, the evolution of a "thing," of a custom, is anything but a progressus toward an end, and even less a logical, direct progressus achieved with the least expense of energy and cost. It is rather a succession of processes of subjugation, more or less profound, more or less independent of one another, that act on the thing. It also includes the resistance offered against each subjugation, the Protean wriggles of defense and reaction, and the results of successful counter-efforts. The form is fluid, but the meaning is more fluid still. Even inside every individual organism it is the same: whenever the whole genuinely grows, the "function" of the single organs shifts. In certain cases the partial perishing of these organs, a reduction in their number (for instance, by the annihilation of the connecting members), can be a symptom of growing strength and perfection. What I mean is this: even partial loss of utility, decay and degeneration, loss of function and purpose, in a word death, belong among the conditions of genuine progressus. Genuine progressus always takes the shape of a will and way to greater power, and is always won at the expense of innumerable smaller powers. A "progress" is measured by the greatness of the sacrifice it demands: humanity as a mass sacrificed to the prosperity of the one stronger species of Man, that would be a progress. I stress this cardinal feature of the historical method all the more because in its essence it runs against the predominant instincts and the prevailing taste. They would much rather put up with absolute casualness, even with the mechanical senselessness of all phenomena, than with the theory of a power-will playing through all phenomena without exception. The democratic idiosyncrasy against everything that rules and wishes to rule, the modern misarchism (to coin a bad word for a bad thing), has gradually dressed itself so thoroughly in the guise of intellectualism, the most abstract intellectualism, that today it penetrates step by step, and has the right to penetrate, even the most exact and apparently most objective sciences. In my view it has already come to dominate the whole of physiology and biology, to their detriment, as is obvious, because it has spirited away a radical idea, the idea of true activity. Under the tyranny of this idiosyncrasy the theory of "adaptation" is pushed to the front of the argument and exploited. Adaptation means a second-class activity, a mere capacity for "reacting"; in fact, life itself has been defined (by Herbert Spencer) as an ever more effective internal adaptation to external circumstances. This definition, however, fails to grasp the real essence of life, its will to power. It fails to see the paramount superiority of those plastic forces of spontaneity, aggression and encroachment, with their new interpretations and tendencies, for which adaptation is only a natural corollary. As a result, the sovereign office of the highest functionaries in the organism itself (among which the life-will appears as an active and formative principle) is repudiated. One remembers Huxley's reproach to Spencer of his "administrative Nihilism": but it is a case of something much more than "administration."

As a result, the sovereign office of the highest functionaries in the organism itself (among which the life-will appears as an active and formative principle) is repudiated. One remembers Huxley's reproach to Spencer of his "administrative Nihilism": but it is a case of something much more than "administration."

[4] English translator’s note: An allusion to Der Zweck im Recht by the great German jurist, Professor Ihering.
reasons: German Species Mensch here denotes stronger type, not biological species.

englishChanges.before: 24. I conclude with three queries, as you will see. "Is an ideal actually set up here, or is one pulled down?" I am perhaps asked.... But have you asked yourselves sufficiently how dear a payment the setting up of every ideal in the world has exacted? To achieve that, how much truth must always be slandered and misunderstood, how many lies must be sanctified, how much conscience must be disturbed, how many pounds of "God" must be sacrificed every time? For a sanctuary to be set up, a sanctuary has got to be destroyed: that is a law. Show me an instance where it has not been fulfilled!... We modern men inherit the immemorial tradition of vivisecting the conscience and practicing cruelty on our animal selves. That is the sphere of our most protracted training, perhaps of our artistic prowess, at any rate of our dilettantism and our perverted taste. Man has for too long regarded his natural proclivities with an "evil eye," so that eventually they have become affiliated in his system to a bad conscience. The converse endeavor would in itself be feasible, but who is strong enough to attempt it? It would be to affiliate to the "bad conscience" all those unnatural proclivities, all those transcendental aspirations contrary to sense, instinct, nature and animalism: in short, all past and present ideals, which are all ideals opposed to life and slandering the world. To whom is one to turn nowadays with such hopes and pretensions? It is just the good men that we should thus bring down about our ears. And in addition, as stands to reason, the indolent, the hedgers, the vain, the hysterical, the tired.... What is more offensive, or more thoroughly calculated to alienate, than giving any hint of the exalted severity with which we treat ourselves? And again, how conciliatory and full of love the whole world shows itself towards us as soon as we do as all the world does, and "let ourselves go" like all the world. For such an achievement we need spirits of a different caliber from what seems really feasible in this age: spirits made potent through wars and victories, to whom conquest, adventure, danger, even pain, have become a need. For it we need to be used to sharp, rare air, to winter wanderings, to ice and mountains literal and metaphorical. We even need a kind of sublime malice, a supreme and most self-conscious insolence of knowledge, which is the appanage of great health. We need (to sum up the awful truth) just this great health!

englishChanges.before: 2. What do ascetic ideals mean? Or, to take one case on which I have often been consulted: what does it mean when an artist like Richard Wagner pays homage to chastity in his old age? In a certain sense he had always done so, of course. But only at the very end did he do it in an ascetic sense. What does this "change of attitude" mean, this radical revolution (for that is what it was)? Wagner swung right round into his own opposite. And what does it mean when an artist swings round into his own opposite? Here, if we are willing to dwell a little on the question, we think at once of the best, strongest, gayest and boldest period that Wagner's life perhaps ever had. It was the time when he was deeply and genuinely absorbed in the idea of "Luther's Wedding." Who knows by what chance we now have the Meistersingers in place of that wedding music? And how much of the one may be an echo of the other? Still, there is no doubt that the theme would have praised chastity. It would certainly have praised sensuality as well; and even so it would have seemed quite in order, and just as Wagnerian. For chastity and sensuality are not necessarily opposed: every good marriage, every authentic, heart-felt love, rises above that opposition. It seems to me that Wagner would have done well to bring this pleasing reality home to his Germans once more, with a bold and graceful "Luther Comedy." There were and are many revilers of sensuality among the Germans, and perhaps Luther's greatest merit is just that he had the courage of his sensuality (it used to be called, prettily enough, "evangelistic freedom "). Even where the opposition between chastity and sensuality really does exist, fortunately it has not needed to be a tragic one for some time now. That should hold for all beings sound in mind and body. They are far from counting their delicate balance between "animal" and "angel" as, on the face of it, one of the principles opposed to existence. The most subtle and brilliant spirits, Goethe and Hafiz for example, have even found in it a further charm of life. Such "conflicts" actually tempt one to live. On the other hand, it is only too clear what happens when these ruined swine are reduced to worshipping chastity (and there are such swine): all they see and worship in it is the opposite of themselves, the opposite of ruined swine. Oh, what tragic grunting and eagerness! Just imagine it. They worship that painful and superfluous contrast which Richard Wagner in his last years undoubtedly wanted to set to music and put on the stage! "For what purpose, forsooth?" we may fairly ask. What did the swine matter to him; what do they matter to us?

englishChanges.before: 5. What, then, do ascetic ideals mean? In the case of an artist we are beginning to see: nothing at all ... or so much that it is as good as nothing at all. Indeed, what use are they? For a long time our artists have not taken a position independent enough, in the world or against it, to make their valuations, or any changes in them, interesting. At all times they have been the valets of some morality, philosophy or religion. Unfortunately they have also often been the inordinately supple courtiers of their clients and patrons, and the inquisitive toadies of the powers that be, or even of the powers still to come. At the very least, they always need a rampart, a support, some authority already in place. Artists never stand by themselves; standing alone goes against their deepest instincts. Thus Richard Wagner, "when the time had come," took the philosopher Schopenhauer as his covering man in front, as his rampart. Who would think it even possible that he could have had the courage for an ascetic ideal without the support of Schopenhauer's philosophy, without the authority of Schopenhauer, which dominated Europe in the seventies? (Here I set aside the question whether an artist without the milk of an orthodoxy could have existed at all.) This brings us to the more serious question: what does it mean when a real philosopher pays homage to the ascetic ideal? I mean a really self-dependent intellect like Schopenhauer, a man and knight with a glance of bronze, who has the courage to be himself, who knows how to stand alone without first waiting for men to cover him in front and for nods from his superiors. Let us look at once at Schopenhauer's remarkable attitude to art, an attitude that even fascinates certain types. For that, obviously, is why Richard Wagner suddenly went over to Schopenhauer (persuaded to it, as is well known, by a poet, Herwegh). He went over so completely that a rift opened, a total theoretical contradiction, between his earlier and his later æsthetic faiths. The earlier was set out, for example, in Opera and Drama; the later in the writings he published from 1870 onwards. Above all, from then on Wagner had no scruples about changing his judgment of the value and position of music itself (and this volte-face is what alienates us most). Until then he had made music a means, a medium, a "woman," who needed an end in order to thrive, a man, that is, the drama. What did he care? He suddenly saw that the novelty of the Schopenhauerian theory could achieve more in majorem musicæ gloriam, that is, through the sovereignty of music as Schopenhauer understood it. Music was abstracted from all the other arts and set against them, as the independent art-in-itself. It did not reflect the phenomenal world as the other arts do. It was rather the language of the will itself, speaking straight out of the "abyss" as the will's most personal, original and direct manifestation. This extraordinary rise in the value of music (a rise that seemed to grow out of the Schopenhauerian philosophy) came at once with an unprecedented rise in the esteem given to the musician himself. Now he became an oracle, a priest, nay, more than a priest: a kind of mouthpiece for the "intrinsic essence of things," a telephone from the other world. From then on he spoke not only music, this ventriloquist of God; he spoke metaphysic. Is it any wonder that one day he spoke ascetic ideals?

englishChanges.before: 9. A certain asceticism, a grimly gay and wholehearted renunciation, is, as we have seen, among the most favorable conditions for the highest intellectualism, and so also for its most natural consequences. It should therefore not surprise us that philosophers in particular have always had a certain fondness for the ascetic ideal. A serious historical investigation shows that the bond between the ascetic ideal and philosophy is tighter and stronger still. One may say that philosophy learned to take its first steps and baby paces only in the leading strings of this ideal — alas, how clumsy, alas, how cross, alas, how ready to tumble and lie on its belly was this shy little darling of a brat on its bandy legs! The early history of philosophy is like that of all good things: for a long time they lacked the courage to be themselves, kept looking around to see whether anyone would come to help them, and were afraid of everyone who looked at them. Just list the particular tendencies and virtues of the philosopher in order: his tendency to doubt, to deny, to wait (to be "ephectic"), to analyze, search, explore and dare, to compare and to equalize; his will to be neutral and objective, his will for everything that is "sine ira et studio". Has anyone yet realized that for quite a long period these tendencies ran against the first claims of morality and conscience? (To say nothing of Reason, which even Luther chose to call Frau Klüglin, the sly whore.) Has anyone yet appreciated that a philosopher who arrives at self-consciousness must feel himself an incarnate "nitimur in vetitum" — and must therefore guard himself against "his own sensations," against self-consciousness? I repeat: it is the same with all the good things we now pride ourselves on. Judged even by the standard of the ancient Greeks, our whole modern life, in so far as it is not weakness but power and the consciousness of power, looks like pure "Hybris" and godlessness. For the very opposites of the things we honor today had conscience on their side for a long time, and God as their guardian. "Hybris" is our whole attitude to nature nowadays, our violation of nature with the aid of machinery and the unscrupulous ingenuity of our scientists and engineers. "Hybris" is our attitude to God — that is, to some alleged teleological and ethical spider behind the meshes of the great trap of the causal web. Like Charles the Bold in his war with Louis the Eleventh, we may say, "je combats l'universelle araignée." "Hybris" is our attitude to ourselves, for we experiment on ourselves in a way we would not permit with any animal, and gladly and curiously we cut open our soul while the body lives. What does the "salvation" of the soul matter to us now? Afterwards we heal ourselves; being ill is instructive, we do not doubt it, even more instructive than being well — inoculators of disease seem to us today even more necessary than any medicine-men and "saviors." There is no doubt that we do violence to ourselves nowadays, we crackers of the soul's kernel, we incarnate riddles who are forever asking riddles, as though life were nothing but the cracking of a nut. And precisely by this we must become, day by day, more and more worthy to be questioned and to question. Perhaps by this we also become worthier to — live?

englishChanges.before: 11. And now that we have caught sight of the ascetic priest, let us take up our problem. What is the meaning of the ascetic ideal? Now it first becomes serious — vitally serious. We now face the real representatives of seriousness. "What is the meaning of all seriousness?" This still more radical question is perhaps already on the tip of our tongue: a question, fairly, for physiologists, which we skip for now. In that ideal the ascetic priest finds not only his faith but also his will, his power, his interest. His right to exist stands or falls with that ideal. No wonder that we run into a terrible opponent here (supposing, of course, that we are opponents of that ideal) — an opponent fighting for his life against those who repudiate it!... On the other hand, it is improbable from the start that so biased an attitude toward our problem will do him much good. The ascetic priest will hardly prove the happiest champion of his own ideal (on the same principle by which a woman usually fails when she wants to champion "woman"), still less the most objective critic and judge of the controversy we have raised. So much is already clear: we shall have to help him defend himself properly against us, rather than fear being too well beaten by him. The idea in dispute is the value our life has from the standpoint of the ascetic priests. They set this life (together with the whole of which it is a part, "Nature," "the world," the whole sphere of becoming and passing away) in relation to an existence of quite another kind, which it excludes and to which it is opposed, unless it denies itself. In that case, the case of an ascetic life, life is taken as a bridge to that other existence. The ascetic treats life as a maze in which one must walk backwards until one reaches the place where it starts; or he treats it as an error which one may, nay must, refute by action, for he demands that he be followed and enforces his valuation of existence wherever he can. What does this mean? Such a monstrous valuation is no exceptional case or curiosity in human history; it is one of the most general and persistent facts there are. Someone who read the capital letters of our earthly life from the vantage of a distant star might perhaps conclude that the earth was the especially ascetic planet, a den of discontented, arrogant and repulsive creatures who never got rid of a deep disgust with themselves, with the world, with all life, and who hurt themselves as much as possible out of pleasure in hurting — presumably their one and only pleasure. Consider how regularly, how universally, how practically at every period the ascetic priest appears: he belongs to no particular race; he thrives everywhere; he comes out of all classes. It is not that he perhaps bred this valuation by heredity and propagated it — the contrary is the case. A necessity of the first order must be what makes this species, hostile as it is to life, grow again and thrive again. Life itself must certainly have an interest in the continuance of such a type of self-contradiction. For an ascetic life is a self-contradiction. Here rules a resentment without parallel, the resentment of an insatiate instinct and ambition that wants to be master, not over some element in life, but over life itself, over its deepest, strongest, innermost conditions. Here an attempt is made to use power to dam the sources of power. Here the green eye of jealousy turns even against physiological well-being, especially against its expression, beauty and joy; while pleasure is felt and sought in abortion, decay, pain, misfortune, ugliness, voluntary punishment, in the exercising, flagellation and sacrifice of the self. All this is in the highest degree paradoxical: we face a rift that wills itself to be a rift, that enjoys itself in this very suffering and grows more and more certain of itself, more and more triumphant, in proportion as its own presupposition, physiological vitality, declines. "The triumph just in the supreme agony": under this extravagant emblem the ascetic ideal has fought from of old. In this mystery of seduction, in this picture of rapture and torture, it recognized its brightest light, its salvation, its final victory. Crux, nux, lux — it has all three in one.

englishChanges.before: 13. But let us turn back. The self-contradiction that seems to show itself among the ascetics, "Life turned against Life," is simply nonsense — this much is absolutely obvious — when judged from the physiological standpoint and not, now, the psychological one. It can only be an apparent contradiction. It has to be a kind of provisional expression, an explanation, a formula, an adjustment: a psychological misunderstanding of something whose real nature could not be grasped for a long time, and whose real essence could not be described. It is a mere word jammed into an old gap in human knowledge. Put briefly, the facts that count against its being real are these. The ascetic ideal comes out of the protective, self-preserving instincts of a decadent life, a life that tries by every means it has to hold its position and fight for its existence. It points to a partial physiological depression and exhaustion, and the deepest, still intact life-instincts keep fighting this ceaselessly with new weapons and new discoveries. The ascetic ideal is one such weapon. So its position is exactly the reverse of what its worshippers imagine: life is struggling in it and through it with death and against death, and the ascetic ideal is a dodge to keep life going. History teaches something important about how far this ideal could rule over man and exercise power over him, especially in every place where the civilization and taming of man was completed. What it shows is the diseased state of man up to now, at any rate of the tamed man: his physiological struggle with death (more precisely, with disgust with life, with exhaustion, with the wish for the "end"). The ascetic priest is the incarnate wish for an existence of another kind, on another plane. He is, in fact, the highest point of this wish, its official ecstasy and passion. Yet the very strength of this wish is the fetter that ties him down here. It is just this that turns him into a tool, one who has to labor to create more favorable conditions for earthly existence, for existence on the human plane. With this very strength he holds the whole herd of failures, distortions, abortions, unfortunates and sufferers from themselves of every kind fast to existence, while he walks instinctively ahead of them as their herdsman. Where does this diseased state come from? For man is more diseased, more uncertain, more changeable and more unstable than any other animal, there is no doubt of it — he is the diseased animal. So where does it spring from? Certainly he has also dared more, innovated more, braved more and challenged fate more than all the other animals put together. He is the great experimenter with himself, the unsatisfied, the insatiate, who fights for supreme mastery against beast, Nature and gods. He is the as yet ever uncompelled, the ever future, who can no longer find any rest from his own aggressive strength, driven mercilessly on by the spur of the future dug into the flesh of the present. How could so brave and rich an animal fail to be also the most endangered, the animal with the longest and deepest sickness among all sick animals?... Yet even this very nausea, this tiredness, this disgust with himself, is thrown off by him with such force that it is at once made into a new fetter. His "nay" to life brings forth, as though by magic, an abundance of graceful "yeas"; and even when he wounds himself, this master of destruction and of self-destruction, it is the wound itself afterward that forces him to live.

englishChanges.before: 14. The more normal this sickliness in man is — and we cannot deny that it is normal — the more honor is owed to the rare cases of psychical and physical powerfulness, the windfalls of humanity, and the more strictly the sound must be protected from that worst of airs, the air of the sick-room. Is that being done? The sick are the greatest danger to the healthy; the strong are harmed not by the strongest but by the weakest. Is that known? Looked at broadly, it is not the fear of man that we should wish to see diminished, not for a minute. This fear forces the strong to be strong and at times terrible, and so keeps the sound type of man intact. What we must fear, what works with a fatality found in no other fate, is not the great fear of man but the great nausea with man, and equally the great pity for man. Suppose these two were one day to be joined in marriage. The maximum of monstrousness would inevitably come into the world at once: the "last will" of man, his will for nothingness, Nihilism. And indeed the road to it is well paved. Anyone who has not only a nose to smell with but also eyes and ears will sniff, almost wherever he goes today, an air something like that of a mad-house or a hospital. I am speaking, as stands to reason, of the cultured areas of mankind, of every kind of "Europe" that there is in fact in the world. The sick are the great danger to man, not the evil, not the "beasts of prey." The ones who are botched, oppressed and broken from the start, the weakest, are the ones who most undermine life under the feet of man, and who instil the most dangerous venom and skepticism into our trust in life, in man, in ourselves. Where shall we escape it, that covert look (which leaves us carrying away a deep sadness), that averted look of the man who was misborn from the beginning, the look that betrays what such a man says to himself — the look that is a groan? "Would that I were something else," this look groans, "but there is no hope. I am what I am: how could I get away from myself? And, verily — I am sick of myself!" Out of such a soil of self-contempt, a veritable swamp soil, grows that weed, that poisonous growth, so tiny, so hidden, so ignoble, so sugary. Here the worms of revenge and vindictiveness swarm; here the air reeks of things secret and unmentionable; here the net of the most malignant conspiracy is forever being spun — the conspiracy of the sufferers against the sound and the victorious; here the sight of the victorious is hated. And what lying, so as never to admit this hate as hate! What a show of big words and attitudes, what an art of "righteous" calumniation! These abortions! What noble eloquence pours from their lips! What a quantity of sugary, slimy, humble submission oozes in their eyes! What do they really want? At any rate to represent righteousness, love, wisdom, superiority: that is the ambition of these "lowest ones," these sick ones! And how clever such an ambition makes them! In fact you cannot help admiring the counterfeiter's skill with which the stamp of virtue, even the ring, the golden ring of virtue, is copied here. They have taken out a lease on virtue absolutely for themselves, these weaklings and wretched invalids, there is no doubt of it. "We alone are the good, the righteous," they say, "we alone are the homines bonæ voluntatis." They stalk about among us as living reproaches, as warnings to us — as though health, fitness, strength, pride, the sensation of power were vicious things in themselves, for which one would someday have to do penance, bitter penance. Oh, how ready they themselves are in their hearts to make others do penance, how they thirst to be hangmen!

englishChanges.before: Among them are plenty of revengeful ones disguised as judges, who forever mouth the word righteousness like a venomous spittle — with mouth, I say, always pursed, always ready to spit at anything that does not wear a discontented look but goes its way in good cheer. Among them, too, is that most loathsome species of the vain, the lying abortions, who make a point of playing "beautiful souls," and perhaps bring to market, as "purity of heart," their distorted sensualism wrapped up in verses and other bandages: the species of "self-comforters" and masturbators of their own souls. The sick man wants to represent some form of superiority, and has an instinct for crooked paths leading to a tyranny over the healthy — where can this will to power of the very weakest not be found? The sick woman especially: no one surpasses her in refinements of ruling, oppressing, tyrannizing. The sick woman, moreover, spares nothing living and nothing dead; she digs up again the most deeply buried things (the Bogos say, "Woman is a hyena"). Look into the background of every family, every body, every community: everywhere you will find the fight of the sick against the healthy. It is mostly a silent fight, waged with minute poisoned powders, with pin-pricks, with spiteful grimaces of patience, but at times also with that diseased pharisaism of pure pantomime which likes best to play the role of "righteous indignation." It can make itself heard right into the hallowed chambers of knowledge, this hoarse yelping of sick hounds, this rabid lying and frenzy of such "noble" Pharisees (I remind readers who have ears once more of that Berlin apostle of revenge, Eugen Dühring, who makes the most disreputable and revolting use of moral refuse anywhere in present-day Germany; Dühring, the paramount moral blusterer there is today, even among his own kidney, the Anti-Semites). They are all men of resentment, these physiological distortions and worm-riddled objects, a whole quivering kingdom of burrowing revenge, indefatigable and insatiable in its outbursts against the happy, and equally so in its disguises for revenge, its pretexts for revenge. When will they really reach their final, fondest, most sublime triumph of revenge? Doubtless when they succeed in pushing their own misery, in fact all misery, into the consciousness of the happy, so that the happy begin one day to be ashamed of their happiness and perhaps say to themselves when they meet, "It is a shame to be happy! there is too much misery!" ... But there could not possibly be a greater and more fatal misunderstanding than for the happy, the fit, the strong in body and soul to begin in this way to doubt their right to happiness. Away with this "perverse world"! Away with this shameful soddenness of sentiment! To stop the sick from making the healthy sick — for that is what such soddenness comes to — ought to be our supreme object in the world. For this it is above all essential that the healthy stay separated from the sick, that they even guard themselves from the look of the sick, that they not even associate with the sick. Or is it perhaps their mission to be nurses or doctors? They could not mistake and disown their mission more grossly. The higher must not degrade itself into the tool of the lower, and the pathos of distance must keep their missions separate to all eternity. The right of the happy to exist, the right of bells with a full tone over the discordant cracked bells, is verily a thousand times greater: they alone are the sureties of the future, they alone are bound to man's future. What they can do and must do, the sick can never do and should never do! But if they are to be enabled to do what only they must do, how can they possibly be free to play the doctor, the comforter, the "Saviour" of the sick?... And therefore good air! good air! and away, at any rate, from the neighborhood of all the madhouses and hospitals of civilization! And therefore good company, our own company, or solitude if it must be so! But away, at any rate, from the evil fumes of internal corruption and the secret worm-eaten state of the sick! So that, indeed, my friends, we may defend ourselves, at least for a while longer, against the two worst plagues that could have been kept in store for us — against the great nausea with man! against the great pity for man!

englishChanges.before: 15. Suppose you have understood in all their depths why it cannot be the business of the healthy to nurse the sick and make them healthy — and I demand that you grasp these reasons profoundly and understand them profoundly. Then it follows that you have grasped a further necessity: the necessity of doctors and nurses who are themselves sick. And now we have and hold, with both hands, the essence of the ascetic priest. We have to accept him as the predestined savior, herdsman and champion of the sick herd; only then do we first understand his awful historic mission. His kingdom is lordship over sufferers; his instinct points him toward it, and in it he finds his own special art, his master-skill, his kind of happiness. He must himself be sick, he must be kith and kin to the sick and the abortions, so as to understand them and come to an understanding with them. But he must also be strong, even more master of himself than of others, impregnable, indeed, in his will for power, so that he can win the trust and the awe of the weak and be their hold, bulwark, prop, compulsion, overseer, tyrant, god. He has to protect them, protect his herds — against whom? Against the healthy, doubtless, and also against envy of the healthy. He must be the natural adversary and scorner of every rough, stormy, unbridled, hard, violently predatory health and power. The priest is the first form of the more delicate animal, which scorns more easily than it hates. He will not be spared a war with the beasts of prey, a war of guile (of "spirit") rather than of force, as is self-evident. In certain cases he will find it necessary to conjure up out of himself, or at any rate to represent in practice, a new type of the beast of prey — a new animal monstrosity in which the polar bear, the supple, cold, crouching panther and, not least important, the fox are joined together in a trinity as fascinating as it is fearsome. If necessity demands it, he will step onto the scene with bearish seriousness, venerable, wise, cold, full of treacherous superiority, as the herald and mouthpiece of mysterious powers. Sometimes he will go even among the other kind of beasts of prey, determined to sow suffering, discord and self-contradiction on their soil wherever he can, and only too sure of his art of being, at all times, lord of sufferers. He brings with him, doubtless, salve and balsam; but before he can play the physician he must first wound. So while he soothes the pain the wound makes, he at the same time poisons the wound. He is well versed in this above all, this wizard and wild beast tamer, in whose presence everything healthy must needs fall ill and everything ill must needs grow tame. He protects his sick herd well enough, indeed, this strange herdsman. He also protects them against themselves, against the sparks of wickedness, knavery, malice and all the other ills that the plaguey and the sick are heir to (sparks that fly even in the center of the herd). With cunning, hardness and stealth he fights anarchy and the ever imminent break-up inside the herd, where resentment, that most dangerous blasting-stuff and explosive, accumulates and accumulates. His real feat, his supreme usefulness, is to get rid of this blasting-stuff in such a way that it does not blow up the herd and the herdsman. If you want the value of the priestly life in the shortest formula, it would be correct to say that the priest is the diverter of the course of resentment. For every sufferer instinctively looks for a cause of his suffering; to put it more exactly, for a doer — to put it still more precisely, for a sentient responsible doer — in brief, for something living on which he can vent his emotions, actually or in effigie, on any pretext. For the venting of emotions is the sufferer's greatest attempt at alleviation, that is to say, at stupefaction: his mechanically desired narcotic against pain of any kind. In this phenomenon alone, according to my judgment, lies the real physiological cause of resentment, revenge and their family — that is, in a demand for the deadening of pain through emotion. This cause is generally sought, but in my view very erroneously, in the defensive parry of a bare protective principle of reaction, of a "reflex movement" at any sudden hurt and danger, just as a decapitated frog still moves in order to get away from a corrosive acid. But the difference is fundamental. In one case the aim is to prevent being hurt any further; in the other the aim is to deaden a racking, insidious, nearly unbearable pain with a more violent emotion of any kind whatsoever, and at any rate for the time being to drive it out of the consciousness. For this an emotion is needed, as wild an emotion as possible, and to excite that emotion some excuse or other is needed. "It must be somebody's fault that I feel bad" — this kind of reasoning is peculiar to all invalids, and the more pronounced the more ignorant they remain of the real cause of their feeling bad, the physiological cause (the cause may lie in a disease of the nervus sympathicus, or in an excessive secretion of bile, or in a lack of sulphate and phosphate of potash in the blood, or in pressure in the bowels that stops the circulation of the blood, or in degeneration of the ovaries, and so forth). All sufferers are awfully resourceful and ingenious at finding excuses for painful emotions. They even enjoy their jealousy and their broodings over base actions and apparent injuries. They burrow through the intestines of their past and present in search of obscure mysteries, where they are free to wallow in a torturing suspicion and get drunk on the venom of their own malice. They tear open the oldest wounds, they make themselves bleed from scars long since healed, and they turn friend, wife, child and everything nearest to them into evil-doers. "I suffer: it must be somebody's fault" — so thinks every sick sheep. But his herdsman, the ascetic priest, tells him, "Quite so, my sheep, it must be the fault of someone; but you yourself are that someone, it is all the fault of yourself alone — it is the fault of yourself alone against yourself." That is bold enough, false enough, but one thing at least is achieved; thereby, as I have said, the course of resentment is — diverted.

In one case the aim is to prevent being hurt any further; in the other the aim is to deaden a racking, insidious, nearly unbearable pain with a more violent emotion of any kind whatsoever, and at any rate for the time being to drive it out of the consciousness. For this an emotion is needed, as wild an emotion as possible, and to excite that emotion some excuse or other is needed. "It must be somebody's fault that I feel bad" — this kind of reasoning is peculiar to all invalids, and the more pronounced the more ignorant they remain of the real cause of their feeling bad, the physiological cause (the cause may lie in a disease of the nervus sympathicus, or in an excessive secretion of bile, or in a lack of sulphate and phosphate of potash in the blood, or in pressure in the bowels that stops the circulation of the blood, or in degeneration of the ovaries, and so forth). All sufferers are awfully resourceful and ingenious at finding excuses for painful emotions. They even enjoy their jealousy and their broodings over base actions and apparent injuries. They burrow through the intestines of their past and present in search of obscure mysteries, where they are free to wallow in a torturing suspicion and get drunk on the venom of their own malice. They tear open the oldest wounds, they make themselves bleed from scars long since healed, and they turn friend, wife, child and everything nearest to them into evil-doers. "I suffer: it must be somebody's fault" — so thinks every sick sheep. But his herdsman, the ascetic priest, tells him, "Quite so, my sheep, it must be the fault of someone; but you yourself are that someone, it is all the fault of yourself alone — it is the fault of yourself alone against yourself." That is bold enough, false enough, but one thing at least is achieved; thereby, as I have said, the course of resentment is — diverted.
reasons: German Kranken und Missrathnen.

englishChanges.before: 17. But is he really a physician, this ascetic priest? We already understand why we are scarcely allowed to call him one, however much he likes to feel like a "saviour" and to be worshipped as one. He combats only the actual suffering, the sufferer's discomfort, not its cause, not the actual state of sickness. This must be our most radical objection to priestly medication. Yet put yourself just once into that point of view, which the priests have a monopoly on, and you will find it hard to exhaust your amazement at all he has seen, sought and found from that standpoint. The mitigation of suffering, every kind of "consoling" — all this shows itself as his very genius. With what ingenuity has he interpreted his mission as consoler, with what aplomb and audacity has he chosen the weapons the part requires! Christianity in particular should be called a great treasure-chamber of ingenious consolations, so great a store of refreshing, soothing, deadening drugs has it piled up within itself. It has hazarded so many of the most dangerous and daring expedients; with such subtlety and refinement, Oriental refinement, it has divined which emotional stimulants can conquer, at least for a time, the deep depression, the leaden fatigue and the black melancholy of physiological cripples. For, speaking generally, all religions are mainly concerned with fighting a certain fatigue and heaviness that has infected everything. You can take it as prima facie probable that in certain places in the world there was almost bound to prevail from time to time, among large masses of the population, a sense of physiological depression. Owing to their lack of physiological knowledge, this did not appear to their consciousness as such, and so its "cause" and its cure could only be sought and tried in the science of moral psychology (this, in fact, is my most general formula for what is generally called a "religion"). Such a feeling of depression can have the most diverse origins. It may result from the crossing of too heterogeneous races (or of classes — genealogical and racial differences also show themselves in the classes: the European "Weltschmerz," the "Pessimism" of the nineteenth century, is really the result of an absurd and sudden class-mixture). It may be brought about by a mistaken emigration, a race falling into a climate for which its power of adaptation is insufficient (the case of the Indians in India). It may be the effect of old age and fatigue (the Parisian pessimism from 1850 onwards). It may come from a wrong diet (the alcoholism of the Middle Ages, the nonsense of vegetarianism — though these have in their favor the authority of Sir Christopher in Shakespeare). It may come from blood-deterioration, malaria, syphilis and the like (German depression after the Thirty Years' War, which infected half of Germany with evil diseases and thereby paved the way for German servility, for German pusillanimity). In such a case a war on a grand scale against the feeling of depression is invariably attempted. Let us inform ourselves briefly about its most important practices and phases (I leave aside, as stands to reason, the actual philosophic war against the feeling of depression, which is usually simultaneous — it is interesting enough, but too absurd, too practically negligible, too full of cobwebs, too much of a hole-and-corner affair, especially when pain is proved to be a mistake, on the naïf hypothesis that pain must needs vanish once the mistake underlying it is recognized — but behold! it does anything but vanish ...). That dominant depression is fought primarily by weapons that reduce the consciousness of life itself to the lowest degree. Wherever possible, no more wishes, no more wants; avoid everything that produces emotion, that produces "blood" (eating no salt, the fakir hygiene); no love; no hate; equanimity; no revenge; no getting rich; no work; begging; as far as possible, no woman, or as little woman as possible; as far as the intellect is concerned, Pascal's principle, "il faut s'abêtir." In ethical and psychological language, the result is "self-annihilation," "sanctification"; in physiological language, "hypnotism." It is the attempt to find some approximate human equivalent for what hibernation is for certain animals and æstivation for many tropical plants: a minimum of assimilation and metabolism in which life just manages to subsist without really entering the consciousness. An amazing amount of human energy has been devoted to this object — perhaps uselessly? There cannot be the slightest doubt that these sportsmen of "saintliness," of whom nearly every nation has at times had an abundance, really found a genuine relief from what they fought with such rigorous training. In countless cases they really did escape deep physiological depression with the help of their system of hypnotism, and their method is consequently counted among the most universal ethnological facts. Similarly it is improper to treat such a plan of starving the physical element and the desires as itself a symptom of insanity (as a clumsy species of roast-beef-eating "freethinkers" and Sir Christophers are fain to do). All the more certain is it that their method can and does pave the way to all kinds of mental disturbances, for instance "inner lights" (as with the Hesychasts of Mount Athos), auditory and visual hallucinations, voluptuous ecstasies and effervescences of sensualism (the history of St. Theresa). The explanation the victims give of such events is always the acme of fanatical falsehood; this is self-evident. Note well, however, the tone of implicit gratitude that rings in the very will to an explanation of such a character. They always regard the supreme state, salvation itself, that final goal of universal hypnosis and peace, as the mystery of mysteries, which even the most supreme symbols are inadequate to express. They regard it as an entry and homecoming to the essence of things, a liberation from all illusions, "knowledge," "truth," "being," an escape from every end, every wish, every action, something even beyond Good and Evil.

englishChanges.before: 19. We have already come to know the ascetic priest's methods: stifling all vitality, mechanical activity, the little joy, and above all the "love your neighbour" herd organization, which awakens the communal consciousness of power to such a pitch that the individual's disgust with himself is eclipsed by his delight in the community's thriving. By modern standards these are the "innocent" methods of fighting depression. Let us turn now to the more interesting subject of the "guilty" methods. They all come down to one thing: producing emotional excess, which serves as the most effective anæsthetic against the depressing state of protracted pain. That is why priestly ingenuity has proved quite inexhaustible in working out one question: "By what means can you produce an emotional excess?" This sounds harsh. Obviously it would sound nicer, and grate less on the ear, if I said instead, if you please: "The ascetic priest always made use of the enthusiasm that lies in all strong emotions." But why go on soothing the delicate ears of our modern effeminates? Why should we budge a single inch before their verbal Pecksniffianism? For us psychologists that would be practical Pecksniffianism in its own right, quite apart from the nausea it gives us. Nowadays a psychologist's good taste (others might say his righteousness) lies, if anywhere, in fighting the shamefully moralized language that smears every modern judgment on men and things. For do not deceive yourself: the chief mark of modern souls and modern books is not lying, but the innocence that comes with their intellectual dishonesty. Meeting this "innocence" everywhere is the most distasteful part of the rather dangerous business a modern psychologist has to take on. It is part of our great danger; it is a road that perhaps leads us straight to the great nausea. I know quite well what all modern books will serve for, and can serve for (granted that they last, which I do not fear, and granted equally that some day there will be a generation with a more rigid, more severe and healthier taste). I know what all modernity will serve for in the eyes of posterity: as an emetic, — and this by reason of its moral sugariness and falsity, its ingrained feminism, which it is pleased to call "Idealism," and at any rate believes to be idealism. Our cultured men of today, our "good" men, do not lie — that is true; but it does them no honor! The real lie, the genuine, determined, "honest" lie (on whose value you can listen to Plato), would be far too tough and strong for them. It would require them to do what people have been forbidden to ask of them: to open their eyes to their own selves, and to learn to tell "true" from "false" in their own selves. Only the dishonest lie suits them. Whatever feels itself a good man can take no other attitude to anything than that of a dishonorable liar, an absolute liar, but none the less an innocent liar, a blue-eyed liar, a virtuous liar. These "good men" are all now tainted with morality through and through, and as far as honor goes they are disgraced and corrupted for all eternity. Which of them could stand one further truth "about man"? Or, to put it more tangibly, which of them could put up with a true biography? Take a few instances. Lord Byron wrote a most personal autobiography, but Thomas Moore was "too good" for it and burned his friend's papers. Dr. Gwinner, Schopenhauer's executor, is said to have done the same; for Schopenhauer also wrote much about himself, and perhaps also against himself: (εἰς ἑαντόν). The virtuous American Thayer, Beethoven's biographer, suddenly broke off his work: he had reached a certain point in that honorable and simple life and could stand it no longer. Moral: What sensible man nowadays writes one honest word about himself? He must already belong to the Order of Holy Foolhardiness. We are promised an autobiography of Richard Wagner; who doubts that it would be a clever autobiography? Think, if you please, of the grotesque horror the Catholic priest Janssen aroused in Germany with his inconceivably square and harmless pictures of the German Reformation. What would people not do if some real psychologist told us about a genuine Luther — told us not with the moralist simplicity of a country priest, or the sweet and cautious modesty of a Protestant historian, but, say, with the fearlessness of a Taine, which springs from strength of character and not from a prudent toleration of strength? (The Germans, by the bye, have already produced the classic specimen of this toleration, and they may well count him as one of their own: Leopold Ranke, that born classical advocate of every causa fortior, that cleverest of all the clever opportunists.)

englishChanges.before: 20. But you will soon understand me. — In short, is there not reason enough for us psychologists never to get free of a certain mistrust of our own selves nowadays? Probably even we are still "too good" for our work. Whatever contempt we feel for this popular craze for morality, we are perhaps none the less its victims, its prey and its slaves; probably it infects even us. What was that diplomat warning us about, when he told his colleagues: "Let us especially mistrust our first impulses, gentlemen! they are almost always good"? This is how every psychologist should talk to his colleagues today. And so we return to our problem, which in fact demands a certain severity from us, a certain mistrust, especially of "first impulses." The ascetic ideal in the service of projected emotional excess: anyone who remembers the previous essay will already partly anticipate the essential meaning packed into these ten words. The thorough unhinging of the human soul, its plunge into terror, frost, ardor and rapture, so that it is freed, as by some lightning shock, from all the smallness and pettiness of unhappiness, depression and discomfort: what ways lead to this goal? And which of them leads there most safely?... At bottom all great emotions have this power, provided they find a sudden outlet — emotions such as rage, fear, lust, revenge, hope, triumph, despair, cruelty. And indeed the ascetic priest has had no scruples about enlisting the whole pack of hounds that rage in the human kennel, unleashing now these and now those. His aim is always the same: to wake man out of his protracted melancholy and chase away, at least for a time, his dull pain and shrinking misery, and always with a religious interpretation and justification to sanction it. Of course this emotional excess has to be paid for afterward — it makes the ill more ill — and so, by modern standards, this kind of remedy for pain is a "guilty" kind.

englishChanges.before: Fairness, however, demands that we stress all the more that this remedy is applied with a good conscience. The ascetic priest has prescribed it in the most implicit belief that it is useful and indispensable — often enough almost collapsing in the presence of the pain he created. Fairness also demands that we stress that the violent physiological revenges of such excesses, and perhaps even the mental disturbances, are not absolutely inconsistent with the general character of this remedy. As we showed previously, it is not meant to heal diseases but to fight the unhappiness of that depression, and its object was to ease and deaden that unhappiness. The object, then, was achieved. The keynote that let the ascetic priest make every kind of agonizing and ecstatic music play on the fibres of the human soul was, as everyone knows, the exploitation of the feeling of "guilt." I indicated the origin of this feeling in the previous essay — as a piece of animal psychology and nothing else: there we met the feeling of "guilt" in its crude state, as it were. Only in the hands of the priest, real artist that he was with the feeling of guilt, did it take shape — oh, what a shape! "Sin" — for that is the name of the new priestly version of the animal "bad-conscience" (the inverted cruelty) — has so far been the greatest event in the history of the diseased soul. In "sin" we find the most perilous and fatal masterpiece of religious interpretation. Imagine man, suffering from himself in some way or other, at any rate physiologically, perhaps like an animal shut up in a cage, unclear about the why and the wherefore! Imagine him in his desire for reasons (reasons bring relief), and again in his desire for remedies, for narcotics at last, as he consults one who knows even the occult — and see, lo and behold, his wizard, the ascetic priest, gives him a hint, the first hint about the "cause" of his trouble: he must search for it in himself, in his guiltiness, in a piece of the past, and he must understand his very suffering as a state of punishment. He has heard, he has understood, the unfortunate man: he is now in the plight of a hen with a line drawn round it. He never gets out of the circle of lines. The sick man has been turned into "the sinner" — and for a few thousand years now we have not been able to get away from the sight of this new invalid, "a sinner" — shall we ever get away from it? — wherever we look, there is the hypnotic gaze of the sinner, always moving in one direction (in the direction of guilt, the only cause of suffering); there is the evil conscience, this "greuliche thier," to use Luther's language; there is rumination over the past, a distorted view of action, the gaze of the "green-eyed monster" turned on all action; there is the wilful misunderstanding of suffering, its transvaluation into feelings of guilt and fear of retribution; there are the scourge, the hairy shirt, the starving body, contrition; there is the sinner breaking himself on the ghastly wheel of a restless and morbidly eager conscience; there are mute pain, extreme fear, the agony of a tortured heart, the spasms of an unknown happiness, the shriek for "redemption." In fact, with this system of procedure the old depression, dullness and fatigue were absolutely conquered, and life itself became very interesting again: awake, eternally awake, sleepless, glowing, burnt away, exhausted and yet not tired — such was the figure of man, "the sinner," once he was initiated into these mysteries. This grand old wizard of an ascetic priest, in his fight with depression, had clearly triumphed; his kingdom had come. Men no longer grumbled at pain, men panted after pain: "More pain! More pain!" So for centuries on end his acolytes and initiates shrieked their demand. Every emotional excess that hurt; everything that broke, overthrew, crushed, transported, ravished; the mystery of torture-chambers, the ingenuity of hell itself — all this was now discovered, divined and exploited, all this was put at the wizard's service, all this helped to bring about the triumph of his ideal, the ascetic ideal. "My kingdom is not of this world," he said, both at the beginning and at the end: had he still the right to talk like that? — Goethe has maintained that there are only thirty-six tragic situations: from that we would infer, if we did not know otherwise, that Goethe was no ascetic priest. He — knows more.

The sick man has been turned into "the sinner" — and for a few thousand years now we have not been able to get away from the sight of this new invalid, "a sinner" — shall we ever get away from it? — wherever we look, there is the hypnotic gaze of the sinner, always moving in one direction (in the direction of guilt, the only cause of suffering); there is the evil conscience, this "greuliche thier,"[4] to use Luther's language; there is rumination over the past, a distorted view of action, the gaze of the "green-eyed monster" turned on all action; there is the wilful misunderstanding of suffering, its transvaluation into feelings of guilt and fear of retribution; there are the scourge, the hairy shirt, the starving body, contrition; there is the sinner breaking himself on the ghastly wheel of a restless and morbidly eager conscience; there are mute pain, extreme fear, the agony of a tortured heart, the spasms of an unknown happiness, the shriek for "redemption." In fact, with this system of procedure the old depression, dullness and fatigue were absolutely conquered, and life itself became very interesting again: awake, eternally awake, sleepless, glowing, burnt away, exhausted and yet not tired — such was the figure of man, "the sinner," once he was initiated into these mysteries. This grand old wizard of an ascetic priest, in his fight with depression, had clearly triumphed; his kingdom had come. Men no longer grumbled at pain, men panted after pain: "More pain! More pain!" So for centuries on end his acolytes and initiates shrieked their demand. Every emotional excess that hurt; everything that broke, overthrew, crushed, transported, ravished; the mystery of torture-chambers, the ingenuity of hell itself — all this was now discovered, divined and exploited, all this was put at the wizard's service, all this helped to bring about the triumph of his ideal, the ascetic ideal. "My kingdom is not of this world," he said, both at the beginning and at the end: had he still the right to talk like that? — Goethe has maintained that there are only thirty-six tragic situations: from that we would infer, if we did not know otherwise, that Goethe was no ascetic priest. He — knows more.

[4] English translator’s note: “Horrible beast.”

englishChanges.before: 22. Wherever the ascetic priest has gained the mastery, he has corrupted the health of the soul, and so he has also corrupted taste in artibus et litteris — he corrupts it still. "So?" I hope I shall be granted this "so"; at any rate, I am not going to prove it first. Here is one solitary indication. It concerns the arch-book of Christian literature, their real model, their "book-in-itself." The Græco-Roman world was splendid, and its splendor included books. Right in the midst of it, face to face with an ancient world of writings not yet fallen into decay and ruin, at a time when certain books were still there to be read, books we would now give half our literature to possess, the simplicity and vanity of Christian agitators (they are generally called Fathers of the Church) dared to declare: "We too have our classical literature, we do not need that of the Greeks." And meanwhile they proudly pointed to their books of legends, their letters of apostles and their apologetic tractlets, just as the English "Salvation Army" today wages its fight against Shakespeare and other "heathens" with an analogous literature. You already guess it: I do not like the "New Testament." It almost upsets me to stand so isolated in my taste about this valued, this over-valued Scripture; the taste of two thousand years is against me; but what does it matter! "Here I stand! I cannot help myself" — I have the courage of my bad taste. The Old Testament is quite another matter; all honor to the Old Testament! In it I find great men, a heroic landscape, and one of the rarest phenomena in the world, the incomparable naïveté of the strong heart; further still, I find a people. In the New, on the contrary, I find just a hostel of petty sects, pure rococo of the soul, twisting angles and fancy touches, nothing but conventicle air, not to forget an occasional whiff of bucolic sweetness that belongs to the epoch (and the Roman province) and is less Jewish than Hellenistic. Meekness and braggadocio cheek by jowl; an emotional garrulousness that almost deafens; passionate hysteria, but no passion; painful pantomime; here manifestly everyone lacked good breeding. How dare anyone make as much fuss about their little failings as these pious little fellows do! No one cares a straw about it — let alone God. And finally they actually wish to have "the crown of eternal life," all these little provincials! In return for what, if you please? For what end? Insolence cannot be carried any further. An immortal Peter! Who could stand him! Their ambition makes one laugh: the creature serves up his most personal life, his melancholies and common-or-garden troubles, cut and dried, as though the Universe itself were obliged to bother about them, for he never tires of wrapping up God Himself in the petty misery in which his troubles are involved. And what about the atrocious form of this chronic hobnobbing with God? This Jewish, and not merely Jewish, slobbering and clawing importunacy towards God! — There are little despised "heathen nations" in East Asia from whom these first Christians could have learned something worth learning, a little tact in worshiping; these nations do not allow themselves to say aloud the name of their God. This seems to me delicate enough; it is certain that it is too delicate, and not only for primitive Christians. For a contrast, just recall Luther, the most "eloquent" and insolent peasant Germany has had, and think of the Lutheran tone in which he felt most in his element during his tête-à-têtes with God. Luther's opposition to the mediæval saints of the Church (in particular, to "that devil's hog, the Pope") was, there is no doubt, at bottom the opposition of a boor. He was offended at the good etiquette of the Church, that worship-etiquette of the sacerdotal code, which lets only the initiated and the silent into the holy of holies and shuts the door against boors. These were definitely not to be allowed a hearing on this planet — but Luther the peasant simply wished it otherwise; as it was, it was not German enough for him. He wished to talk directly, to talk personally, to talk "straight from the shoulder" with his God. Well, he has done it. The ascetic ideal, you will guess, was at no time and in no place a school of good taste, still less of good manners — at best it was a school for sacerdotal manners: that is, it contains in itself something that was a deadly enemy to all good manners. Lack of measure, opposition to measure, it is itself a "non plus ultra."

englishChanges.before: With all their noisy agitator-babble, however, they get nowhere with me. These trumpeters of reality are bad musicians; their voices do not rise from the depths audibly enough, they are not the mouthpiece of the abyss of scientific knowledge — for today scientific knowledge is an abyss — and the word "science" in such trumpeter-mouths is a prostitution, an abuse, an impertinence. The truth is just the opposite of what the ascetic theory maintains. Science today has absolutely no belief in itself, let alone in an ideal above itself. And wherever science is still made of passion, love, ardor and suffering, it is not the opposite of the ascetic ideal but rather the incarnation of that ideal's latest and noblest form. Does that sound strange? There are plenty of brave and decent working people, even among the learned men of today, who like their little corner. Just because they are pleased to be there, they sometimes become indecently loud in demanding that people today should be quite content, especially in science — for in science there is so much useful work to do. I do not deny it. There is nothing I should like less than to spoil these honest workers' delight in their handiwork, for I rejoice in their work. But the fact that science requires hard work, and that it has contented workers, is no proof at all that science as a whole has one end, one will, one ideal, one passion for a great faith today. The contrary, as I have said, is the case. When science is not the latest manifestation of the ascetic ideal — and such cases are so rare, so select and so exquisite that they cannot affect the general judgment — science is a hiding-place for every kind of cowardice, disbelief, remorse, despectio sui, bad conscience. It is the very anxiety that springs from having no ideal, the suffering from the lack of a great love, the discontent with an enforced moderation. Oh, what does science not cover today? How much, at any rate, does it not try to cover? The diligence of our best scholars, their senseless industry, their burning the candle of their brain at both ends, their very mastery in their handiwork: how often is the real meaning of all that to keep themselves from continuing to see a certain thing? Science as a self-anæsthetic: do you know that? You wound them — everyone who associates with scholars experiences this — you sometimes wound them to the quick with a perfectly harmless word. When you think you are paying them a compliment, you embitter them beyond all bounds, simply because you lacked the finesse to work out what kind of customers you had to deal with: the sufferer kind (who won't own up even to themselves what they really are), the dazed and unconscious kind who have only one fear — coming to consciousness.

englishChanges.before: 26. Or does the whole of modern history, perhaps, show more confidence in life and in its ideals? Its loftiest pretension today is to be a mirror. It rejects all teleology and wants no more "proving." It disdains to play the judge, and shows its good taste in that. It asserts as little as it denies; it fixes, it "describes." All this is ascetic to a high degree, yet nihilistic to a much higher degree; make no mistake about this! In the historian you see a gloomy, hard, but determined gaze, the eye of an isolated North Pole explorer (perhaps so as not to look within, so as not to look back?). There is snow; life is silenced here; the last crows that caw here are called "whither?", "Vanity," "Nada." Nothing more flourishes or grows here, except at most the metapolitics of St. Petersburg and the "pity" of Tolstoi. Then there is that other school of historians, a perhaps still more "modern" school, voluptuous and lascivious, which ogles life and the ascetic ideal with equal fervor, which wears the word "artist" like a glove, and has by now secured a "corner" for itself in all the praise of contemplation. Oh, what a thirst these sweet intellectuals arouse, even for ascetics and winter landscapes! Nay! The devil take these "contemplative" folk! I would much rather wander with those historical Nihilists through the gloomiest, grey, cold mist! Nay, I shall not mind listening (supposing I have to choose) to someone completely unhistorical and anti-historical (a man like Dühring, for instance, whose periods have intoxicated a hitherto shy and unavowed species of "beautiful souls" in contemporary Germany, the species anarchistica within the educated proletariate). The "contemplative" are a hundred times worse. Nothing has ever made me so intensely nauseous as one of those "objective" chairs, one of those scented mannikins-about-town of history, a thing half-priest, half-satyr (Renan parfum). The high, shrill falsetto of his applause betrays what he lacks and where he lacks it: it betrays where the Fates, in his case, have plied their ghastly shears, alas! in too surgeon-like a fashion! I find this distasteful, and it tries my patience. Let him stay patient at such sights who has nothing to lose by it. For me the sight is enraging; such spectators embitter me against the "play," even more than the play itself does (history itself, you understand). Anacreontic moods come over me imperceptibly. This Nature, who gave the steer its horn and the lion its χάσμ ὀδοντων: for what purpose did Nature give me my foot? — To kick, by St. Anacreon, and not merely to run away! To trample on all the worm-eaten "chairs," the cowardly contemplators, the lascivious eunuchs of history, the flirters with ascetic ideals, the righteous hypocrites of impotence! All reverence from me to the ascetic ideal, in so far as it is honorable! So long as it believes in itself and plays no pranks on us! But I do not like all these coquettish bugs, whose insatiable ambition is to smell of the infinite until at last the infinite smells of bugs. I do not like the whited sepulchres with their stagey imitation of life. I do not like the tired and the used up who wrap themselves in wisdom and look "objective." I do not like the agitators dressed up as heroes, who hide their dummy-heads behind the stalking-horse of an ideal. I do not like the ambitious artists who would fain play the ascetic and the priest, and are at bottom nothing but tragic clowns. I do not like, again, these newest speculators in idealism, the Anti-Semites, who roll their eyes in the patent Christian-Aryan-man-of-honor fashion today, and with moralist attitudes and agitation dodges so cheap that they exhaust any patience, try to rouse all the blockhead elements in the populace (the unfailing success of every kind of intellectual charlatanism in present-day Germany is tied to the almost indisputable and already quite palpable desolation of the German mind. I look for its cause in a too exclusive diet of papers, politics, beer and Wagnerian music, not forgetting the condition this diet presupposes: the national exclusiveness and vanity, the strong but narrow principle "Germany, Germany above everything," and finally the paralysis agitans of "modern ideas"). Europe today is above all wealthy and ingenious in means of excitement; it apparently has no more pressing need than stimulantia and alcohol. Hence the enormous counterfeiting of ideals, those most fiery spirits of the mind; hence also the repulsive, evil-smelling, perjured, pseudo-alcoholic air everywhere. I should like to know how many cargoes of imitation idealism, of hero-costumes and high-falutin' claptrap, how many casks of sweetened pity liqueur (Firm: la religion de la souffrance), how many crutches of righteous indignation to prop up these flat-footed intellects, how many comedians of the Christian moral ideal would have to be exported from Europe today before its air smelled pure again. It is obvious that this over-production opens up a new trade possibility, and obvious that a new business is to be done in little ideal idols and obedient "idealists" — don't pass over this tip! Who has the courage? We hold in our hands the possibility of idealizing the whole earth. But what am I saying, courage? Here we need only one thing — a hand, a free, a very free hand.
