englishChanges.before: 27. Enough! Enough! Let us leave these curiosities and complexities of the modern spirit, which provoke as much laughter as disgust. Our problem, the problem of the meaning of the ascetic ideal, can certainly do without them. What has it to do with yesterday or today? I shall deal with those matters more thoroughly and severely elsewhere (under the title "A Contribution to the History of European Nihilism"; I refer here to a work I am preparing: The Will to Power, an Attempt at a Transvaluation of All Values). I bring them up here for one reason only. Even in the most intellectual sphere, the ascetic ideal has at times just one real kind of enemies and damagers: the comedians of this ideal, because they awaken mistrust. Everywhere else the mind works seriously, powerfully and without counterfeiting, and there it dispenses altogether with an ideal (the popular name for this abstinence is "Atheism"), except for the will for truth. But this will, this remnant of an ideal, is, if you will believe me, that very ideal in its severest and cleverest formulation, esoteric through and through, stripped of all outworks; so it is not so much the ideal's remnant as its kernel. Unqualified honest atheism (and we, the most intellectual men of this age, breathe no other air) is not as opposed to that ideal as it seems. It is rather one of the last phases in the ideal's evolution, one of its syllogisms and pieces of inherent logic. It is the awe-inspiring catastrophe of a two-thousand-year training in truth, a training that finally forbids itself the lie of the belief in God. (India saw the same course of development, quite independently, and so with some demonstrative value: the same ideal driving to the same conclusion, with the decisive point reached five hundred years before the European era, or more precisely at the time of Buddha. It began in the Sankhyam philosophy, and Buddha then popularized it and made it into a religion.)

englishChanges.before: What has really triumphed over the Christian God? I ask the question with all strictness. The answer stands in my Joyful Wisdom, Aph. 357: "the Christian morality itself, the idea of truth taken with ever-increasing seriousness, the confessor-subtlety of the Christian conscience translated and sublimated into the scientific conscience, into intellectual cleanness at any price. To regard Nature as though it were a proof of the goodness and guardianship of God; to interpret history in honor of a divine reason, as a constant proof of a moral order of the world and a moral teleology; to explain our own personal experiences, as pious men have for long enough explained them, as though every arrangement, every nod, every single thing were invented and sent out of love for the salvation of the soul: all this is now done away with. The conscience is against it, and every subtler conscience regards it as disreputable, dishonorable, as lying, feminism, weakness, cowardice. By this severity, if by anything at all, we are good Europeans and heirs of Europe's longest and bravest self-mastery.". .. All great things bring about their own ruin by an act of self-dissolution: so wills the law of life, the law of necessary "self-mastery" even in the essence of life. The law-giver is always finally exposed to the cry, "patere legem quam ipse tulisti." So Christianity went to ruin as a dogma, through its own morality; and so Christianity must go to ruin again today as a morality. We are standing on the threshold of this event. Christian truthfulness draws one conclusion after another, and at last it draws its strongest conclusion, the one against itself. That happens when it puts the question: "what is the meaning of every will for truth?" And here I touch again on my problem, on our problem, my unknown friends (for as yet I know of no friends). What sense has our whole being, if not that in us that will for truth has become conscious of itself as a problem? — With this self-consciousness of the will for truth, morality from now on goes to pieces; there is no doubt about it. This is that great hundred-act play reserved for the next two centuries of Europe, the most terrible, the most mysterious, and perhaps also the most hopeful of all plays.
